speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Besides reliving part of my formative years, among thousands of other middle-aged fans doing the same, I got a chance to see ageing rockers put on a spectacular show.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More recently, my sister joined another 50,000 Singaporeans at the concert more aligned to her musical tastes – the Korean girl band, Blackpink.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, as much as both my sister and I enjoyed our outings, the shadow of the failed Sports Hub's public-private partnership (PPP) hung over the scene.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We were left to wonder the future of this crowning jewel of our local sporting scene, left to hosting concerts by foreign musical acts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, I am old enough to recall a time when the stadium hosted the Kallang Roar.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It was a time when a deep sense of nationalism welled up as we supported, especially, the football team.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My mother still relates a story of me falling off the bed as a baby after being startled by a roar following Quah Kim Song's winning goal in the 1977 Malaysia Cup final.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The stars of my time, Fandi Ahmad, V Sundramoorthy and David Lee, united Singaporeans across ethnic lines in a way that top-down policies can only dream of inspiring.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the Roar has fallen silent, as has the facility that was meant to revitalise local sports.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In today's Motion filed by myself and my fellow friend and sports fan, Faisal Manap from Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC), we hope to provoke an earnest debate on the challenges faced by our national sportsmen and women, whether they represent the country at the highest levels or if they are young aspirants seeking a healthy outlet for their time and energy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, my opening speech will focus on the economic challenges faced in bringing Singapore sport to the next level, using, in particular, the Sports Hub episode as a foil.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Mr Faisal will tackle what he and the Workers' Party believe are the non-economic challenges, using the example of football – the closest that we have to a national sport – to illustrate his points.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But we also hope that the discussion will go beyond just sports alone, because an eye to looking at our relative weaknesses on this front can offer insight into other areas of policy in Singapore, where we have been far less successful on the global stage despite our outpouring of blood and treasure to stoke greater success.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Every medal took sweat and tears and I ask this House to join me in a round of applause to all our athletes whether they medalled or not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should not forget, however, that she did so amidst a continuing battle with the burden of injuries and the pressure of immensely high expectations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Fencer Tay Yu Ling returned to the top of the podium in fencing after retiring in 2010, proving that even in sport, age can just be a number that should not limit the boldness of our dreams.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Runner Soh Rui Yong, who had been excluded in the 2021 Games, earned a silver medal in the 10,000 metres.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: During the event, Soh had offered Indonesian rival Rikki Simbolon a drink after the latter had missed his in a striking mark of sportsmanship.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our para-athletes, despite the physical odds that they face, once again did us proud.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They brought home 44 medals in total, with Colin and Sophie Soon contributing a fifth of the total haul.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As much as we celebrate the achievements of these athletes, we should also be aware of where we have fallen short.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But unless we can candidly look at both the wins and losses, we cannot fully understand what we must do to get better.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, every successful sportsperson or team goes through the very same post-mortem after a competition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given that we rank ninth in terms of population in the region, perhaps one could credibly argue that we outperformed our small size.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But population is only one factor in determining cross-country sports outcomes – and not even the most important one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If anything, systematic analysis suggests that it is countries' income that is far more influential, whether in specific sports like soccer or across sports more generally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, some have even gone as far as to argue that the same socio-economic determinants, especially wealth and development, drive sporting success.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is a simple reason why incomes matter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Richer countries are better able to channel significant public and private resources towards sporting achievements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, it is unsurprising that the quality of supporting infrastructure matters, too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is a prima facie reason why we might wish to promote infrastructure, such as the Sports Hub, as a catalyst to elevate local sport.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It also underscores the need to prioritise soft infrastructure, such as athlete support and coach development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In that regard, Singapore has, unfortunately, not only punched below our weight but has actually consistently gotten worse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL Parliament app.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I traffic in charts and figures, but I will walk us through this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The top panel shows a plot where the logarithm of the total medal count in the Summer Olympics is set against per capita incomes, measured in a common currency that is corrected for inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The small blue dots are other countries across the different competitions since 1976.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The green line is the best-fit line from a simple linear regression.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The way to read it is that observations above the line are over-achievements for their level of per capita income and vice versa for those below.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We are far below, consistent with clearly falling short.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: While our lack of Olympic success turns out to be not that unusual among ASEAN nations, we remain unambiguously an outlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: A similar story can be told for our lack of football success, which is shown in the bottom panel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But here, we are now talking about a ranking, where a low number is better and so the line is inverted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Yet, here, our story is even more disappointing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Our FIFA ranking back in 1993 is right smack on that green line, which means that we were at least consistent with our level of development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But as we have gotten richer, our ranking has, paradoxically, slid further away from where we would otherwise expect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What explains our nation's anomalous outcomes is that it turns out money alone is not enough.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Countries that have prioritised sporting achievement, including at the highest level, note that this prioritisation is what is important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is why tiny Uruguay can win the World Cup twice and still consistently send competitive teams to the tournament.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is why Iceland's 330,000 people can qualify for international basketball and football tournaments and why Australia is a powerhouse in swimming, Jamaica keeps tearing up the tracks and the All Blacks represent New Zealand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Part of the grand plan to revitalise our local sporting scene was the Singapore Sports Hub.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The Sports Hub was conceived as a PPP that was meant to go far beyond infrastructure provision.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Its bid evaluation placed a weight of two-fifths on appeal of sports, leisure and entertainment programming – more than any other criteria – reflecting the importance that the Government placed on operational considerations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This came after a "detailed financial, legal and operational due diligence" effort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But it is notable that symptoms of underlying problems were already presenting themselves right from the start.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Even after construction, operational issues plagued the project.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: A football friendly between Brazil and Japan held in 2014 received criticism that the pitch was "more sand than grass." Just two months later, a Jay Chou concert held at the Hub was plagued by a leaky roof.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In 2016, rumours swirled about how one of the consortium partners was at risk of being ejected and a fiasco for that year's National Day Parade, which included a proposed upcharge for extra rehearsal days, poor reviews of the venue and a final price tag around twice the cost of that of the Floating Platform or the Padang.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Throughout, the facility had gone through Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) like hot potatoes, averaging one every other year, not to mention others in the c-suite.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But if these fundamental problems were known to the Government, it did not telegraph much of this to the rest of us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But we should be clear about why we pursued a PPP in the first place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Beyond the simple-minded desire to flow with a public policy fad, in principle, there are three reasons why one may pursue a PPP for a given project.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: First, it is because the public sector does not have sufficient funds, and a partnership with the private sector becomes a means of unlocking necessary financing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is often the case with infrastructure projects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Governments grant the rights of levying usage charges for, say, a road or bridge, to a private developer in exchange for their delivering the said construction project.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Second is because the desire to share the risks of the project between two parties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: For projects with uncertain economic prospects, such as those who wish to build power or water treatment plants, especially in the still-developing area, roping in private partners can diversify the risks of potential losses among those with the ability and the willingness to bear such risks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: There is potentially a third area where PPP may appear to make sense but, in reality, warrants much more careful consideration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is when the private sector may appear to possess the necessary expertise in the area, perhaps due to superior knowledge of the technology or the market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But is it truly necessary to adopt a partnership structure where the upside from risks undertaken are mutually shared?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What does the private sector contribute to the endeavour beyond their skills?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Do the partners expand the market, develop the business?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: After all, if it is expertise alone, a superior model would be to simply hire the necessary human resources, project by project.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: You can think of the same thing when a firm decides on hiring workers, it takes a special contributor to be conferred the benefits of partnership.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: For those unfamiliar with the model, it is easy to lay a criticism on it, but this is, to be fair, misguided.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is like blaming the tools on the poor workman.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Moreover, we have extensive empirical evidence documenting the success of PPP projects in infrastructure, health and education across a wide variety of performance indicators both at home as well as worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Such projects include desalination and NeWater plants here and incineration plants, residential and university accommodation and even a whole tertiary campus – ITE College West.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In addition to the Sports Hub, the tender for Changi Motorsports Hub was investigated by the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB) in 2011.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But the path not taken may perhaps be just as revealing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In 2016, the Government ruled out a PPP for Changi Terminal 3 because it did not wish to focus on profits at the expense of service standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: A similar motivation appeared to be behind the abandonment of the PPP for NUS University Town where the ability to price services would be severely constrained by the overall desire to ensure subsidised higher education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Such sentiments are instructive because they underscore the importance of looking beyond purely financial considerations to the ultimate purpose of any given project.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: As Minister Edwin Tong explained in his Statement to Parliament following the takeover announcement, the Government was aware of the options available but it chose a PPP over the traditional procurement route anyway.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We can probably rule out the first of the major justifications I outlined earlier for adopting a PPP, which is that there were financing constraints.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: After all, this Government – unlike, say, one of our higher education institutions – would generally have no difficulties raising the necessary funds for a major infrastructure project, especially one that contributes to key national objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: As proof of the pudding, this Government routinely raises amounts for key infrastructure projects that are far larger than just $1.3 billion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The reason seems more aligned with the third justification, which is that the partnership might have availed of specialised expertise, presumably for operating the Hub.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But as I explained, we wish to tread carefully when deciding on a partnership to leverage expertise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: While such skills may well be lacking at home, it remains unclear why we did not simply put such foreign talents on the payroll.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We routinely bring in consultants, experts and managers even in areas where we have some expertise in, such as in finance or technology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Besides, the all-important operational partners of the SportsHub PPP were either local or had been based here for an extended period: venue operations fell under Global Spectrum Pico, a tie-up that includes a local company, and its facilities management was overseen by DTZ, whose presence in Asia is due to another Singaporean firm, Edmund Tie.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Perhaps, then, it comes down to the second justification, which is a desire to share risks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: My best guess is that this was, indeed, a prime motivator.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In trying to offload risks, but still retaining its non-pecuniary objectives, the Government was trying to have its cake and eat it, too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Was the Government trying to get the private sector to bear the financial risks, and then turning around and insisting that it also accommodates social objectives, instead of just concentrating on the bottom line?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And imposing fines for unmet standards that it cannot be expected to meet, would that not further sour the partnership?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Such an approach where the Government can shift risks to the private sector while reaping benefits without active management is, I am afraid, naïve optimism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is well understood that PPPs are ill-suited for social infrastructure since profit-making and social objectives may frequently diverge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In fact, a study reveals that appropriate risk allocation and sharing is one of the top three critical success factors behind PPP projects in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This disconnect was recognised by those involved in the running of the SportsHub.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Insiders shared about problems, such as too many potentially conflicting KPIs and stakeholders, excessive top-down oversight with little agency offered to SportsHub management and possibly misaligned goals even among key Government agencies, such as SportsSG, the Singapore Tourism Board and the Economic Development Board.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And since we do want our country's sports jewel to ignore our nation's sports promotion and community-building activities, having the Government assume both the role of client and controller means that the PPP arrangement was arguably fundamentally untenable to begin with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Now that the Government has entirely taken over the Sports Hub, it is valuable for us to ask if it plans to ensure that the facility fulfils the aspirations for catalysing Singapore Sport, as we had truly hoped it would, close to a decade and a half ago.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Here, I will pose a series of questions, which I hope the Minister could offer more insight into.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: First, how will Government management differ in practice from the PPP model?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: One reason that the Government offered for pursuing the PPP approach in the first place was that it did not have the expertise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: What assures us that it has the expertise now to successfully run a world-class sports and events venue?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If it does not – and I am sympathetic to how we should not necessarily expect civil servants to possess such talent – will we then go the route of hiring external experts and, if so, why was this not done in 2008?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: More generally, will the Government commit to clear objectives that are aligned in advance among stakeholders?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It strikes me that a consultation process can help us better understand what the public has with regard to a proper and ideal use of the facility since it is meant to inspire local sports participation after all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Second, how does the Government plan to balance community uses with profitable enterprises?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: For example, will there be a revision to venue rentals now that the Government has taken over the Sports Hub?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In particular, will there be a distinction between commercial rental and community ones?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: After all, one reason why the substantial takeover fees were paid was ostensibly to remove commercial barriers for local sports promotion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Minister Tong has already alluded to some of these in his earlier speech under the rubric of ActiveSG and Kallang Alive, including "National School Games, Singapore Youth Festival performances", and possibly even the "National Day Parade".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: He even hoped for a "return of the casual stroller or jogger to the stadium".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If the concern is understandably the crowding out of commercial returns due to the latter, we could perhaps consider scheduling community use events during clear downtimes when the facilities are not being used.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But if, indeed, the Government will not operate the Sports Hub under the same assumptions as SHPL, how much does it expect to incur on an annual basis for operation in the years ahead and how will this differ from the original sums paid to SHPL?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This discussion of numbers naturally leads us to a more careful discussion of sport expenditures in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: To do this, we must step back and scrutinise the budget just a little bit, so that we are working off a common context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I promise I am not going to circulate any more handouts, but I will quickly summarise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But there are additional operational costs of $800 million which will have to be incurred through till 2035.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am assuming that these will be accounted for on an annual basis and will show up in the Budget Statements in future, but I am happy to stand corrected if I am incorrect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If we agree with these numbers, then the next step is to ask if such expenditures should be giving us more bang for the buck.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: As it turns out, the general expenditure on recreational and sporting services for the EU as a whole amounted to 0.7% of all general government expenditure, a share very similar to ours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Japan spends a mere 0.02%, and yes, you heard that right, of its government budget on sport.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And in Korea, the entire Ministry of Culture, Sport and Tourism, which notably includes massive expenditures on promoting Korean culture via Hallyu, comes to only 1.3% of the national budget, with sports accounting for just 0.3%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Yet, these countries have performed more admirably on the international sporting stage than we have, even taking into account their larger populations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Ironically, we are ranked the best in the world for a sport, tchoukball, that does not have a national association.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: For another sport without a recognised national association, dodgeball, Singapore is sixth or seventh.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But all this applies at the micro level as well, which is why the Sports Hub example is illuminating.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Both Dennis Tan and Faisal Manap will speak about football.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, Mr Leon Perera will go on to highlight some less celebrated sports, although along the way, he will also speak more generally about how our sports ecosystem may be strengthened.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Mr Gerald Giam will do likewise, offering ideas on tweaking the local youth ecosystem to help improve our odds of sporting success in the international arena.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And Ms He Ting Ru will, similar to Leon, speak about inclusion in our sporting system, including the disabled and those who are not necessarily participating at the highest levels of sporting competition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I look forward as well to all the other contributions from Members of this House, in what I expect to be a lively debate on how we can take Singapore sports to its next level.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I salute all our Team Singapore athletes for giving their best, sacrificing time and energy, and for their resilience and endurance in overcoming challenges and obstacles in flying our Singapore flag high.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My heartiest congratulations go out to our medal winners for their triumph and bringing pride to our country, also to our national athletes who had bettered their personal bests at the Games as well as those who fought hard against formidable opponents.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A big thanks to our Team Singapore's coaches and officials and a deep appreciation to our athletes' families, loved ones and friends for their great support and encouragement in spurring and motivating our athletes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For the 32nd SEA Games and 12th ASEAN Para Games, we celebrated the continued success of our swimmers both at the SEA Games and the Para Games and we rejoiced at the resurgence of runner Shanti Pereira – among other wonderful wins.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But there were also moments of despair, in particular, when we saw our football team suffer their heaviest SEA Games loss in decades when they lost 7-0 to Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Our footballers' dismal showing at the SEA Games came not long after another crushing disappointment when we limped out of the ASEAN Football Federation (AFF) Championships 2022 tournament.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It felt like rubbing salt to the wound or, in Malay, "sudah jatuh ditimpa tangga", or a double whammy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I can confidently say that football has the strongest following among Singaporeans as compared to any other sport.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Football is also known to be a unifying sport as it brings together the different segments of society, regardless of socio-economic status, race, language and religion.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: While this is not unique to Singapore, our football culture has its unique characteristics.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We have our Kallang Roar and Kallang Wave, named for the location of our former National Stadium, where fans always turned out in droves to support our Lions in every home match when they competed in the Malaysian League and Cup competitions.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: That experience fostered a sense of our shared bonds and a feeling of oneness and pride of supporting our national teams, as each fan became a part of the Kallang Roar and Wave.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Sadly, Madam, this experience now feels like ancient history.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We have not witnessed such exhilarating and tremendous support for our Lions for many years.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many are still painfully waiting for the revival of our Lions, expressing our concerns, sharing views and perspectives, but, regrettably, there are quite a big number who have lost faith and given up after our Lions' poor performance in AFF Championships 2022 and the 32nd SEA Games, followed by two recent uninspiring international friendlies.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Speaking in support of this Motion, I would like to again surface mine as well as fellow Singaporeans' observations, concerns, thoughts on the current situation and what can be done for the future of our football.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Some of these points are a reiteration and elaboration of what I have said in this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My speech is a small contribution in terms of observations and perspectives in our attempts to Make Singapore Football Great Again.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: To begin with, let us look at where Singapore currently stands in the Federation Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) rankings.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The highest ranking we ever attained was 73rd in 1993, while the lowest is 173rd in 2018 and our average is 127th.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Since we hit bottom in 2018, we improved by 15 places in five years.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But this minor improvement is a small consolation for the players and fans who are struggling to understand how we have failed to improve over the years despite all the efforts put in.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Our recent results demonstrate that where many other countries in the region have improved, Singapore football has fallen behind.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We need to see what had worked and what did not work in the past, so that we can dissect, review, finetune and come up with the best efforts and measures in improving our football.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe any changes that need to be made should start with setting of a Goal or Vision for Singapore Football.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe that both the Football Association of Singapore (FAS) and the Government understand this.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In 1998, then-Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong had this vision, Goal 2010, to qualify for the World Cup in that year.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We obviously did not make it, but we had a brief glimmer of hope when our junior Lions won third place during the inaugural Youth Olympic Games (YOG) hosted in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: That team, coached by former player Kadir Yahaya, seemed to hold promise for a brighter future in Singapore football.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I will speak more on that unfulfilled promise later.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: More recently, in August 2019, it was reported in the media that the then-Vice President of FAS, Mr Edwin Tong mentioned that, I quote, "FIFA World Cup 2034 will be a realistic goal for Singapore." On this matter, I had asked the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) through a Parliamentary Question in September 2019, as well as in my Committee of Supply (COS) 2020 cut on FAS' strategic plans in achieving this goal.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: MCCY's replies were that the Ministry was waiting for FAS to advise them on their plans.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, in March 2021, FAS, as reported in the media, shared that the World Cup 2034 is an "aspirational target".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Pertaining to World Cup 2034, I would like to seek two clarifications.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One, FAS has announced in August 2019 that World Cup 2034 is a realistic goal.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Meanwhile, in March 2021, FAS set it as an "aspirational target".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Can FAS or MCCY confirm whether it is the former or the latter?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But surely, there has to be more to the roadmap.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If we cannot even advance beyond the group stages in regional competitions, making it to the World Cup is nothing short of a fantasy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And even if, by some miracle, we were to meet that unlikely aspirational target, we are likely to be utterly humiliated.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We have never made it past the qualifying rounds on our own steam.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Let us set our sights on the AFC Asian Cup and develop a roadmap towards that goal.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The roadmap can include milestones, such as winning the AFF Championship and maybe even gold at the SEA Games in a decade.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In this manner, there is greater accountability as well.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And if we need to revisit the strategy along the way and tweak it here and there, so be it.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is better than setting an aspirational target that is plain unrealistic.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Once again, as I did in my COS 2022 speech, I welcome the small steps that have been taken under the UTR project, such as the setting up of School Football Academies and partnerships with global leaders in football, such as clubs from the Spanish premier La Liga.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is not the first time that FAS has tried to implement youth development programmes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One example is the Junior Centres of Excellence (JCOEs) which were implemented in 2011.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If we go back further, we have the Milo Soccer School.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For those who may be too young to remember, the Milo Soccer School was a key youth development programme in the 1980s and 1990s which gave birth to many of our nation's football heroes, among whom are Fandi Ahmad, Nazri Nasir and Lee Man Hon.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: So, we know that youth development is not a new idea for Singapore football.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But we also have to confront our failures in youth development, despite the investment of time and resources.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In 2015, then-FAS technical director Michel Sablon, in a media report, praised JCOEs and mentioned that with further improvement of this programme, he was confident that Singapore's national team can be like Japan's by 2020.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Maybe Mr Sablon was being over-enthusiastic in speaking to the media; maybe his sense of optimism was hopelessly misplaced.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: What we do know is that we have failed to make progress in youth development even after all the programmes that were implemented and even after we appointed several reputable technical directors and coaches.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There was a time in the 1970s and 1980s when our football team was on par with the current Asian football powerhouses, such as the Japanese and Korean teams.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The relative lack of progress suggests that there are factors that hindered the effectiveness of our plans and programmes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These could include failures in the training and development system and the lack of quality in mentoring, coaching and grooming our young talents.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: To elaborate this point further, I would like to return to our 2010 Singapore Youth Olympic Games (YOG) team, which I mentioned earlier in my speech.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This team created history for our football when they won a bronze medal at the tournament.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And they seemed to hold great promise, having also secured a 3-2 victory over the Tottenham Hotspur academy team during the team's two-week camp in England in their preparation for YOG 2010.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The players from that tournament were dubbed a "Golden Generation" not only for achieving a milestone bronze medal at the inaugural event, but also for their exciting style of play.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And yet, a review of their fortunes a decade later told a story of a lost generation of footballers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: First quote: "After the YOG, there was no follow-up… We had no coach and we didn't even have a single training session for seven or eight months".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Another quote, "While much was promised, in terms of on-the-ground work, nothing was really done.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We were on our own, things soon went downhill, and eventually they forgot about us".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, I believe we need to pose some hard questions, identify where we have previously gone wrong and rectify these errors as we commit towards a long-term youth development programme that will not lead to another "Golden Generation" turning into a "Lost Generation".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There are other, less positive, unique aspects to Singapore football which we need to address if we are to progress towards success.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In 2019, I noted that former national player and coach Fandi Ahmad had made reference to a "unique ecosystem" in Singapore football which he felt was important for the coach of our national team to understand.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In response to Fandi's comments, FAS had cited our small population, land constraints and the competing commitments, such as National Service and academics, which our young players have to juggle, compared to their peers globally and regionally, who are more likely to be full-time professionals.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe these "unique" factors remain relevant today.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In my previous speech, I had called on MCCY, SportSG and FAS to form a unique team to examine how we can leverage these factors to create a more positive ecosystem for our footballers and, in fact, all our athletes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The issue of National Service has been thoroughly debated in this House and I acknowledge the various allowances for deferment or disruption of National Service obligations which the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) has provided for our athletes competing at a high level.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Balancing our defence needs with our sporting aspirations is necessary and possible.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A country with a population of around four million, it has been achieving great success in international football.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Another point I would like to share which could spur our football is about providing better support in terms of employment or career path for our national players upon their retirement from football.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I brought this up as I met and spoke to a couple of Singapore's ex-internationals who shared that they do not encourage their children to pursue their dreams to start a football career.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: When asked why, their short reply, "No future." Their concern is what would become of their children after their short career stint in football.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Baihakki gave assurance that our aspiring footballers of the next generation would see football as a viable career which does not end once they hang up their boots.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The sporadic and occasional closed door consultations FAS has held is of limited value and has the risk of creating an echo chamber.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, I would propose that this review does not only look into our dismal performance at the SEA Games but instead do a review of Singapore football as a whole, a review that will look into making Singapore football great again.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And if it means we need to tear down FAS and rebuild from the ground up, so be it.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As I have mentioned in the earlier part of my speech, football is a unifying sport as it brings together the different segments of society regardless of socio-economic status, race, language and religion, making Singapore football great again will bring the revival of Kallang Roar and the Kallang Wave which our nation has been patiently waiting for almost three decades.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I also join my Workers' Party colleagues, Members of this House and all Singaporeans in extending our well wishes to Team Singapore athletes who competed at the Southeast Asian (SEA) Games and the Southeast Asian (SEA) Paralympic Games last month.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At every international sporting event, a few Singaporean athletes stand out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the last SEA Games, Shanti Pereira's name was on everyone's lips and deservedly so, as she took her place as the fastest sprinter in Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Feng Tianwei's grit was a source of pride for many at her swan song at the last Commonwealth Games.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And there are certainly athletes who wish they could have done better.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To these sportsmen and women, I say: failure makes future success even sweeter; so, stay in the fight and know that Singapore will always be rooting for you.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I want to express my support for the national Under-22 football team which could do with more support from everyone right now.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A few results during the SEA Games may have been hard to swallow, but I look forward to Singapore football putting this tournament behind them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are a few sports that can unite Singaporeans nationally like football can.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We saw that during the 2020 Suzuki Cup semi-final when the Lions, with the team down to eight men, fought hard, despite the odds.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In doing so, they earned the respect of so many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Sportsmen and women have that incredible gift, the ability to lift their compatriots in a way very few expressions of human achievement can.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That is the incredible unifying power of sports and why our athletes, regardless of their sport, play a huge role in nation-building and deserve our support and utmost respect.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On a more personal note, I would like to congratulate Aljunied-Hougang Town Councillor, Mr Francis Seet and his daughter Tiffany.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Right off the bat, it is important to recognise that there are certain obligations involved when an athlete competes under the national flag.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, as they are highly competitive individuals, it is not unusual to find that sports attract its fair share of the strong-minded and the strong-willed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, this element of their character is sometimes the "X" factor that also pushes them to surpass their opponents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: History is replete with such headstrong characters, such as the great Muhammad Ali, whose showmanship both in and out of the ring and incredible ability combined to define him.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To say that he routinely thumbed his nose at authority is probably an understatement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In March 1966, he consciously objected to being drafted to serve in the Vietnam War and earned the ire of those in authority, which he referred to as the "white establishment".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: His sense of universal justice was captured for posterity in his famous words, "Why should they ask me to put on a uniform and go 10,000 miles from home and drop bombs and bullets on brown people in Vietnam, while so-called Negro people in Louisville are treated like dogs and denied simple human rights?" Arising from his personal stand against the war, he was systematically denied a boxing licence in every state in the US and stripped of his passport.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a result, he did not fight professionally from March 1967 to October 1970, when he was aged 25 to almost 29 – the best years of his sporting life – as his legal battle worked its way through the US criminal justice system until his conviction was overturned in 1971.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In many sports, people wear their hearts on their sleeves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore's recent past, national footballer Noh Alam Shah was one such individual.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Whenever I can, like many Singaporeans, I make it a point to watch the Singapore Lions in action.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Noh Alam Shah gave his heart and soul when in national colours.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But he had a temperamental side and was involved in violent conduct – conduct which cannot be condoned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After Singapore's 7-0 loss to Malaysia in football at the last SEA Games, much fan frustration was directed at the management team of FAS.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One commentator on Instagram told the current FAS Acting President Bernard Tan to resign.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Bernard Tan responded by challenging the individual to meet face-to-face, something he later apologised for.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Given the emotions involved in sport and the popularity of football in Singapore, I can understand Mr Tan's passion, even as it was always going to be matched by some of our long-suffering football fans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We can all accept that sport ignites passions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We win together, we lose together, we celebrate together and we hurt together.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I wish to speak about the Singapore National Olympic Council (SNOC)'s non-selection of long distance runner Soh Rui Yong for the upcoming Asian Games.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My last substantive communication with him was to congratulate him on his performance at the recently concluded SEA Games.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He had previously won the gold medal for Singapore in the marathon at the SEA Games, both in 2015 and 2017.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: His latest non-selection will seriously curtail his ability to run and medal for Singapore ever again.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Unlike fixed term suspensions for violent conduct or criminal offences, SNOC's blanket non-selection forces his sporting career into limbo for an unknown period.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirty-six pages of documents allegedly leaked to The Straits Times detailed posts and comments that SNOC took issue with.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: According to a Rice Media article dated 17 June this year which was titled, "Soh Rui Yong isn't perfect and he should not have to be", Rui Yong responded to SNOC's objection by removing the post in question.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This did not placate SNOC and he was still not selected.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The same article says that Rui Yong was not given a chance to clarify his post before the SEA Games' Appeals Committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He was quoted as saying, "I look forward to proving myself on the track and I hope the Committee would see sense in putting me on the team for the Asian Games.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And on my part, I also endeavour to be more careful." The Olympic Charter states that National Olympic Committees' selection of athletes shall not just be based on sporting performance, but an ability to serve as an example to the sporting youths of one's country.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I wish to restate that it is not unreasonable for SNOC to expect our sportsmen and women to exhibit discipline.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: SNOC must have the authority to bar athletes after a disciplinary panel has heard the affected athlete out, consistent with the principles of natural justice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But I ask that SNOC take a more forgiving attitude towards Soh Rui Yong.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, SNOC has a track record of forgiving athletes that have fallen short of being examples for our sporting youths and allowed them to compete for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Both these athletes were involved in criminal offences.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, why is SNOC's attitude towards Rui Yong different?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The core of the schism between SNOC and Rui Yong appears to be a spat that arose when Rui Yong challenged the SNOC's nomination of another athlete for an International Sportsman award.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Rui Yong disputes the nomination as a matter of principle, I would think, and he disagrees with the facts put forward.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A very senior SNOC figure testified in a civil trial against Rui Yong and senior management figures in Singapore sports had made online posts criticising Rui Yong's actions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is a widespread belief that the latest non-selection is a carry-over of that original spat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One cannot help but feel that things have turned personal, with SNOC taking a far stronger stand against Rui Yong, compared to other athletes who have committed transgressions as if to teach him a lesson for his outspokenness.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The current impasse makes everyone look like who they are really not.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: SNOC has done much work in promoting Singapore sports, bringing sponsors on board and raising the esteem of sports in the minds and hearts of Singaporeans and many parents in a very big way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe that politicians should not be directly involved in sports and, when they do get involved, it would be for such purposes – as a facilitator to raise the profile of our sports and sportsmen, generating support from corporates, society and parents, and to bring some much-needed wisdom and equanimity into disputes, such as those involving Rui Yong and SNOC.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For their part, I am of the view that our sports administrators can afford to take an elevated approach as they have done in the past and be more big-hearted, especially when you consider their collective seniority and contributions to Singapore sports.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To begin with, a more enlightened and mature approach from all but, particularly SNOC – which does not just hold all the cards but is, clearly, the party in which the power relationship between athlete and state representation resides – can make a massive difference.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope this matter can be brought to an amicable resolution with better engagement by a mediator from the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I ask the Minister to take the initiative and support my call.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our sporting ecosystem is strengthened when we focus on sporting values, sportsmanship and bringing glory to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I support the Motion filed by Member for Sengkang Jamus Lim and Member for Aljunied Muhamad Faisal Manap.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Their tenacity and determination embody the Singapore Spirit, a nation that, indeed, punches above its weight.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Sports, as I impart them to my students, are a mirror that reflects a nation's vitality.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It unveils the determination, unity and resilience within us – serving as a source of national pride and a catalyst for community cohesion.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Reflecting on my journey, first as an athlete, then as a Physical Education teacher, then as a Sports Science lecturer, and now as a Member of Parliament, I have seen the transformational powers of sports.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is in the joyful shouts and cries of children playing in the school fields and school halls, the tense moments as you await your race in the track and field competition, that community spirit, that feel that you get at a sports competition.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Sports bring us together, teach us about resilience and inspire us to push our boundaries.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our sporting ecosystem should, therefore, be perceived not merely as a conveyor belt for medals, prospects but as a vibrant platform that unites us.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Community sports are the cornerstone of our sporting ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our champions, like Fandi Ahmad, Joseph Schooling and Shanti Pereira, amongst many others, first kindled their passion and honed their skills within the confines of our schools, our local sporting facilities and community centres.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The National School Games serve as a crucial platform for fostering this development.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This annual competition incites the competitive spirit among our young athletes and provides an early stage for talent identification.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But the significance of community sports surpasses the discovery of sporting talent.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It cultivates a sporting culture permeating our society, bolsters social cohesion and instils a shared sense of identity and pride.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When children pass the baton in a relay race or collaborate in a game of sepak takraw, they are not merely playing; they are acquiring teamwork, discipline and resilience.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These unconventional sports introduced in schools are gaining traction due to their dynamic and inclusive nature.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Despite their growing popularity, these sports often do not receive the same level of support or recognition as more traditional sports.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They serve as an important vehicle for stress relief and mood improvement, especially among our youths.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But we must acknowledge and address the mental health challenges faced by our athletes, too, who often deal with immense pressure.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This underlines the need for a well-resourced sporting ecosystem and justifies further backing for community sports and emerging sports.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In doing so, we are not just nurturing future champions but investing in the mental health of our population.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And our national "Unleash the Roar!" project speaks to this, in the context of football.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To uplift the standards of Singapore football, we need to first grow a broad base of participation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our children have many options to play football today, even though our void decks are out of bounds due to safety – our school fields, our halls, the parks, the School Football Academies, ActiveSG Football Academy, Singapore Sports School, private clubs and academies – they are all available.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: From this broad base, we need to systematically identify the best talent for further development.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In that regard, it is important that we equip our coaches and scouts to do this well.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Identified talents need to undergo structured training and development.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, we also need a high-level competitive league that our local young players, as well as the best players from the region, aspire towards.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And this is where I come to the Singapore Premier League (SPL).

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To me, sporting success extends beyond the medals we secure on international platforms; it is deeply rooted in the strength and vibrancy of our community sports culture.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about nurturing unity, fostering resilience and creating a platform for everyone to maximise their potential.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: There is no linear or predetermined process for success.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a dynamic process, constantly shaped and reshaped by multiple factors.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It emerges from the interaction of the individuals, that is, our athletes; the task, which is the sports they are in; and the environment, which is the community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In that regard, "Success is an emergent property of the interaction between an athlete and their community itself." And as we venture into the next decade, let us embrace this dynamic, interdependent relationship within our sporting ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my view, sporting success transcends the accumulation of medals on the international stage and is a multifaceted achievement that encompasses community involvement, personal growth and the manifold benefits that ripple through our society.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I support the Motion as moved by my hon colleague and Member of Parliament for Sengkang GRC, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, "that this House celebrates the accomplishments of our athletes and para-athletes at the recent 32nd SEA Games and the 12th ASEAN Para Games in Cambodia, and calls on the Government to undertake a thorough evaluation of the areas of improvement in Singapore's sporting ecosystem, and commit to realising clear, achievable goals for sporting success over the coming decade." Indeed, I join my colleagues and Members of the House in congratulating our athletes and para-athletes at the recent SEA Games and ASEAN Para Games in Cambodia.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to congratulate all the athletes from Hougang Single Member Constituency (SMC) for their achievements and thank them for their hard work and dedication.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In addition to the points he has made, I also have a few suggestions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We have a massive following of European football and many in Singapore have a favourite English Premier League team or a European club.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many Singaporeans were disappointed with the results of our football team at the SEA Games, and we saw much outpouring of emotions by many.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many of us wondered how we have gotten to where we are today.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, beyond the disappointment and frustrations, I believe there is national will to see Singapore football succeed and we want to support our players and coaches to improve and succeed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I believe we can do more to increase accessibility to the sport and, therefore, cultivating a larger pool of talents and increase buy-in from Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To begin with, I think it is important to develop a broader base of talent.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While we can understand why there may be some disparities, I think FAS can still do more to invest in its own lower football leagues or what FAS described as "domestic football leagues" in its notes to their financial statements for Financial Year 2022.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope FAS can do more to generate interest, increase participation and improve standards.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There should be more equitable distribution for these lower grassroots leagues under FAS to provide a larger pool of talent for SPL clubs as well as for our national team.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If such grassroots football leagues had even one-fifth of such resources dedicated to them, the conditions and levels of grassroots football can improve drastically.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, clubs can have more budget for training spaces and coaches or even simpler things like having more balls for matches and decent insurance coverage for their players.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Still on the issue of the funding of SPL clubs, which I have mentioned earlier, I would also like to suggest that such funding may be a two-edged sword.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While it is encouraging that clubs can afford to pay their players and keep the lights on, it appears to have its drawbacks in other aspects.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, there is no pressing need to market themselves, to reach out to new fans and cultivate a strong fanbase to support each club.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, football fans want to support teams that have history and identity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, Futbol Club (FC) Barcelona attracts fans with a tiki-taka brand of football, and even a club like Stoke City, which garnered a cult following in 2010 with their physical brand of football.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While having a common pool of funds for the club is good on paper, it may, in fact, dilute the identity factor.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In fact, this may, in turn, improve their advertising and sponsorship income.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Another possible solution is to earmark specific funds for purposes, such as marketing, merchandising and ticket subsidies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Another suggestion is to gradually reduce the general funding over a longer period of time, say, 10 years, to encourage clubs to find diverse revenue streams.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Earlier, I mentioned the disparity of funding between SPL and SFL clubs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This would encourage greater competition among all clubs at all levels and enhance quality, standards, participation and interest at all levels.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It will drive clubs in lower leagues to improve their standards and seek promotion to the SPL.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It will discourage complacency for clubs at the SPL level as they cannot take their higher grant or income stream for granted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many household names that football fans of all ages recognise, started out with street football – from Diego Maradona to Johan Cruyff and, perhaps more recently, players like Ronaldinho, Wayne Rooney or Cristiano Ronaldo.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many Singaporeans of different generations would remember playing football at void decks or even on grass patches in the kampung.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How has our street football culture developed over the decades?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our street football culture in Singapore has been curtailed by the lack of space.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the earlier years, perhaps we had a unique void deck football culture when neighbours of even both genders would come together to have a kickabout.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It was near home, it was sheltered, so people can play, rain or shine, and it has many pre-made goal posts or teammates in the form of pillars.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, as our municipal management culture made advances, "No Football" signs would dampen the playing of football at void decks, and understandably so, in consideration of safety, cleanliness and noise, before HDB eventually stopped building suitably sized void decks in our HDB blocks in the past 20 years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There are, of course, commercial futsal courts appearing in the past 20 years as an alternative, such as The Cage and The Rainforest, but these have their own barriers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is impractical for primary school children to travel to these places alone with their friends, fork out the money and organise their own matches.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even for many adults, the travel and the need to look for sufficient teammates make this a rather formal affair that requires a high degree of organisation instead of the pick-up games in the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While there are designated street courts in some neighbourhoods, the weather in Singapore is an active deterrent for play during the afternoon, which is when many children may have their free time after school or homework.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Perhaps, we can revive the void deck football culture in a more modern manifestation by recreating the conditions that made void deck football so inviting – the close proximity to home, the shelter from the rain and the sun, and the ease of access.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, FAS can also do more to encourage having more five- or seven-a-side games or tournaments for youth football.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Five- or seven-a-side games or tournaments, together with the necessary skills training, may be especially appropriate for youth football, such as for those aged 16 and below, before the players' full physical maturity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This has been recognised by footballing powerhouses, such as England, Germany, even FIFA and, locally, at FAS.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, this comes at the risk of leaving behind late developers who cannot match their peers physically earlier on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They do not have the same opportunity or access to resources as their peers who hit puberty earlier.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This has been used by the New Zealand All Blacks rugby team to create success.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This has also been used in the English Premier League (EPL).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Studies have shown that bio-banding results in a more technical and challenging game.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I will submit that adopting bio-banding will further complement the current youth development programme's emphasis on improving tactical and technical skills.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While researching in preparation for this speech, I was reminded that even FIFA themselves set in stone rules that enforce this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We have many illustrious experts in the field and we need to trust them to bring Singapore football to the next level.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We owe a profound debt of gratitude to our athletes who proudly fly the Singapore flag in tournaments like the SEA Games and Para Games.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They have sacrificed through their long hours of training and through rising to the challenge of intensely competitive sports where they might face the agony of defeat as easily as the thrill of victory.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For our athletes, we must not only be passive spectators.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We must, on occasions like this Parliamentary Sitting, honour them with the respect they deserve for their efforts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But as we honour and respect our athletes for what they have done in the past, we must be bold to set ambitious goals for the nation's sporting future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This speaks to the second part of the Motion by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Faisal Manap.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We must strive to enhance our sports ecosystem such that our athletes will find sports a rewarding and sustainable career and that there can be a thriving, commercially attractive ecosystem for other stakeholders, including commercial sponsors and advertisers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: First of all, Madam, what kinds of goals do we want to set for sports nationally?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For every country, there would always be a tension across various goals, for example, cultivating peaks of excellence versus encouraging mass participation, or shining the spotlight on our local athletes while also seeking economic benefits from global leagues and foreign athletes and teams.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This means providing a baseline of support, encouragement and publicity for all sportspersons, including para sportspersons, spanning both those who are successful and those who are less so.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To do justice to those resources, such efforts have to involve regular, hard-nosed reviews of the successes and failures of past policy, such as what my colleague Mr Faisal Manap called for earlier in the context of FAS.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, to apply our communications machinery to highlight our athletes' success and inspire mass participation in sports, which has health and many other benefits.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, to convert that mass interest and participation deriving from sporting excellence into a vibrant business ecosystem whereby the sports industry and its athletes can derive a larger share of revenues from the private sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This last goal is particularly important if we want to make the sports industry sustainable and attractive to athletes, other sports industry professionals and commercial participants versus being an excessively Government-dependent industry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The last goal is probably where we need the most work.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We have to attract strong audiences and spending, which, in turn, will attract commercial sponsorship, participation and advertising, which, in turn, can generate the money needed to spark more excellence, in a virtuous cycle.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It does not make sense to speak of a commercial strategy when there is no audience interest.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The horse has to come before the cart.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Sports like football, badminton, tennis and golf, for example, have a mass audience worldwide and command strong interest in Singapore, too.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, there are less well-known sports where Singaporean athletes have achieved great results regionally and even globally.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We have a national champion in this sport.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Paul Lim is recognised as one of the best darts players in the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: His story is an interesting one, the story of a person fuelled by passion without necessarily having the backing of resources.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In a story in TODAY Online from 2017, Paul recounted that in the early part of his journey in darts, he struggled. "I decided to quit my job and go to work on the American circuit.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I worked part-time as a chef from Monday to Thursday, then from Friday to Sunday, I would play tournaments.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For my first two years, I had no sponsors and I depended on my savings and my job." Paul excels in the soft-tip darts world, which he picked up two decades ago.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Soft-tips are plastic which allows for the scoring to be done automatically.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Matches can be played online via the electronic dartboards.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This makes it more player-friendly, which, in turn, draws a huge younger crowd that is willing to spend.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But agitation creeps into his voice when the state of the local steel-tip scene is brought up. "I feel really angry," he said, and I am quoting from the article here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is from Paul: "We could have been growing in the steel-tip (competitions) too, but it's just that the people who ran the (Singapore) Darts Association, for the last 10 years have run it to the ground." We used to send teams to the World Cup, organise the Singapore Open, Pesta Sukan, had a great league system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It was great in the early days. "We have good players … but they can't go nowhere, that's a shame, really." Without an association to be affiliated with, players are unable to represent Singapore internationally.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that SportSG does provide support for athletes in sports where there is no NSA, but it begs the question why there is no NSA and more concerted efforts in a field like darts, where we have world-class athletes and, hence, the potential to build on that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, let me talk about e-sports, an industry at the early stages of growth world-wide.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Given the tremendous commercial potential for this sport, it deserves the kind of close analysis of success and targeted support that I spoke about.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am glad that there is an NSA for this sport, unlike darts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, in e-sports, Singapore won a SEA Games gold medal for Valorant, albeit not without some controversy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a sport deserving of more media attention and one where our top performers can hopefully get support in attracting emulators.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, it is telling that a Yahoo News article from 2021 said that "Unlike Olympic athletes, our e-sports heroes don't usually get prime time coverage in the media".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Two names worthy of mention here are Daryl "iceiceice" Koh and Ho Kun Xian, who is known simply as Xian.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They are some of Singapore's best e-sports athletes that have been champions of multiple globally renowned competitions with the biggest significant tournament earnings in their careers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Daryl reportedly made over US$1.7 million in tournament earnings alone last year, excluding salary and sponsorships.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is the support they receive from the Government proportionate to their sporting success and are determined efforts being made to build a viable ecosystem, with new players entering who are inspired by these greats?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Also, e-sports refers to a collection of various games with different publishers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are different titles, such as DotA, CSGO, Fortnite, Call of Duty and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Why does the Singapore E-Sports Association limit its support only to certain games?
