speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While Singapore has recently won a SEA Games medal for Valorant, why was there no representation for other games, such as DotA 2 and CSGO, which have not only some of the biggest prize pools globally but have also hosted huge events in Singapore, such as the International, and have a large and devoted local fan base?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: She achieved 200.5 kilogrammes, ahead of Noemie Allabert and Shizuka Rico.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The brothers Matthew and Marcus Yap have also managed a string of achievements in powerlifting.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2017, Matthew set a powerlifting squat world record, 215.5 kilogrammes, in the Under-66kg sub-junior category at the Asian Classic Powerlifting Championships.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: According to Ms Daphne Loo of Powerlifting Singapore as reported in an article in The Straits Times, "Having worked 10-hour shifts at a Korean eatery and saving their allowances just to be able to make this trip to Belarus to compete, there was no way they could afford a flight back.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They had already spent $5,500 for the chance to win the World Record," Ms Loo wrote.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The article said that as Powerlifting Singapore was then not an NSA, there is no funding to send athletes overseas.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Even today, there still remains uncertainty about the sport and the funding they can expect to receive from governing bodies, as reported in a September 2022 article in TODAY.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, let me move to cuesports, starting with billiards.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We have a world-class athlete in Peter Gilchrist, who won the World Billiards Championship (English billiards) in 1994, 2001, 2013 (long format) and 2019.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Peter was a two-time Sportsman of the Year in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We also have Aloysius Yapp, who was the world junior champion in nine-ball in 2014 and runner-up in the 2021 US Open Pool Championship.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2022, Aloysius won a bronze medal at the World Games in Birmingham, Alabama, for nine-ball.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: He reached No 1 in the world rankings in 2021.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I note that Cuesport Singapore has received some Government funding.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are a number of other lesser-known sports where we have great talent in Singapore and where more can be done to capitalise on that talent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the interest of time, I cannot delve deep into all these, but I will refer to them briefly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our sailors also won three of the nine gold medals on offer at this year's SEA Games in Cambodia.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In bowling, Singaporean Cherie Tan was named World Bowling Athlete of the Year by the World Bowling Association in 2019.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Shayna Ng won the International Bowling Federation Super World Championships women's singles title in 2021.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As my hon friend Assoc Prof Jamus Lim mentioned, we also do well in tchoukball and dodgeball, being among the top 10 in the world, even though these sports do not have NSA-level recognition and support.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We clearly have some outstanding talent in less well-known sports at the global or regional level, people like Aloysius Yapp and Peter Gilchrist in billiards, Paul Lim in darts, “iceiceice” and Xian in e-sports, Farhana Farid and the Yap brothers in powerlifting, and Shayna Ng and Cherie Tan in bowling, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We ought to apply ourselves to do a few things as a country in regard to these lesser-known sports.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, our sports administration professionals at SportSG and the NSAs should try to unpack the reasons why we have such top talents, remove unnecessary layers of bureaucracy where it is called for, and help tweak our ecosystem to replicate such factors more broadly – the availability of certain types of training or attachment opportunities abroad, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I will move on to the third part of my speech, which is on identifying top talent that can perform at the highest levels in the region and the world at an early stage.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What else can we do to make sure we are identifying such talent early and supporting them with the resources that are necessary to achieve excellence in competitive sports today?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In contrast to the ancient Greek Olympic ideal – and perhaps disappointingly some might say – sporting excellence these days is, to a considerable extent, a function of financial investment in the best coaches, research and analytics, equipment, sports medicine doctors, sports massage therapists, even sports psychologists and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I suspect that not many Singaporean families have that amount to spend or would be willing to spend that on a sporting career for their children if they did.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the case of Joseph Schooling, he did receive state funding, but this came later in his career, after he had already started getting some good results in the US.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As his uncle Max wrote in a public post quoted in a Mothership article: "His travel was not paid for by "state money" but by his parents.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: His fees at a very expensive school – chosen because it was a school that specialised in combining academic and sporting excellence in swimming – were paid for not by "state money" but by his parents.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: His accommodation in North Florida was not paid for by "state money" but by his parents.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The same source of "money" was what paid for his specialist coaches, his trips to various competitions and so on." In fact, according to Max, state money began to flow only very late in the game.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As Joseph himself said in a TODAY article from 2016, "   bsolutely not (enough financial support).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Which parent should have to pay over US$1 million out of their own pocket to help their kid succeed?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Multi-million-dollar Awards Programme is really nice if you hit the target, but without support and funding, how do you hit those goals?" In an interview with CNA in November last year, Joseph said, "As far as financial support goes, I definitely think the associations can do a better job.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We don't really have much funding." There is a bit of chicken-and-egg problem here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Here, we should direct funding drawn not only from the state but also philanthropic donors as well as corporate sponsors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But we need to place our bets well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In doing this, we need rigorous, scientific early-stage identification of potentially amazing athletes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Do we currently have a good enough infrastructure and system to spot amazing talent at an early age?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: After all, the science of sports has advanced a great deal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is now significant academic and published literature on how future potential can be predicted to a considerable extent by performance metrics and facts determined scientifically at an early age.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is something SportSG should strive to do and discuss more openly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, are our sports teachers primed with the necessary training to identify revealing predictive metrics and to be able to escalate such cases for national attention?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Are they trained to differentiate someone with the potential to become truly great as opposed to just above average?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I note that for many professional sports in the US and Europe, there is literally a professional vocation known as talent scout.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These professionals are highly trained, held to clear KPIs and fly around extensively to spot talent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Do we have a system for doing this?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If we succeed in attracting audience numbers and companies to certain sports where we do well, we will also need business managers who know how to optimise the business ecosystem to make it attractive and sustainable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such skills and best practices are available in abundance in countries like the US and the UK, where sports are, in many cases, a thriving, profitable, multi-billion-dollar industry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There must be enough money in the ecosystem to attract and retain good people.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, there are certain types of artistic and creative activity where it is hard to achieve full commercial viability anywhere in the world – symphony orchestras, for example, and certain types of classical art forms, museums and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In these industries, state funding will probably remain key, though, even here, efforts can be made to draw in philanthropic donations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But in sports, commercial viability is not a futile goal, as examples around the world demonstrate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I trust the debate today will generate many useful discussions and will spark public participation in the conversation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need the Singaporean people to wholeheartedly shape and thus support our sporting directions and to walk with our sporting stakeholders to make the future for sports and our sportspersons in Singapore better than the past.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: One was Sprint queen Shanti Pereira, who was also commended by fellow Members.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: At 26 years old, Shanti became the first Singaporean woman to clinch gold medals for both the 100-metre and 200-metre sprint events and rewrote the national sprint records several times this year.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: He clinched gold at the games and broke the national and SEA Games record for 50-metre freestyle.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With this winning time, Jonathan has also qualified for Paris Olympics 2024.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: His achievements are impressive even though he is still currently serving his National Service.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Izaac swept three gold medals in all three table tennis men’s events by beating competitors who are more than twice his age.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: At the 12th ASEAN Para Games, our athletes won 12 golds, 15 silvers and 17 bronzes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Special acknowledgement must be given to swimmer siblings, Colin and Sophie Soon, who both excelled.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They clinched gold medals and rewrote the Games records for the S13 freestyle event.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For a small nation to compete with more populous neighbours, it is not an easy feat.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: But we did well and what was achieved is credible, to say the least.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Even with these accomplishments, I am of the opinion that there is always more room to achieve sporting successes as a nation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The fundamentals for this blueprint are in place, we are on the right track and there are bright sparks.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With the recent achievement as a reference, it is likely that in another decade or so, we might be able to see more TeamSG athletes on the Olympics podium.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And in order to achieve sporting successes, focus must be placed on youth development.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These are significant investments to assist our high-performance athletes with a conducive training environment and to provide some financial support for them to train and compete at major competitions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In October 2021, I spoke about nation-bonding through sports in Parliament and I recommended a four-pronged approach to strengthen our competitive sports system.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The four points were: (a) focus on a few key sports; (b) search for talents from a young age; (c) nurture them through training and competitions; and (d) help them persevere through the challenging periods.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These approaches will require commitment and continual efforts from both the Government and stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: STTA was founded in 1931 and has a long history of more than 92 years.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The association has gone through its fair share of ups and downs over the years.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Today, table tennis is one of the most popular sports in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many Singaporeans would remember how the Singapore women’s team won our first Olympics silver medal in the Beijing Olympics 2008.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There were criticisms with regard to the fact that they were foreign talents.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, their contributions have undeniably elevated the standard of competitive table tennis in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To add, our head coaches for our current national team were both former Olympians: Coach Jing Junhong and Coach Gao Ning.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They are naturalised Singaporeans and have remained here to help STTA nurture our national paddlers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Their valuable experiences and skills have contributed towards our table tennis successes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Experienced stalwarts like Olympians Feng Tianwei, Yu Mengyu and Lin Ye have retired and STTA will have to ensure that there are new talented paddlers to take over.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The recent Cambodian SEA Games men’s team gold medal was a historic win.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It was the first victory in 50 years by an all local-born team.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This achievement is a strong testament to the early fruits of our local youth development efforts.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In STTA, we have put in place a very stringent selection process and start training the paddlers at a very young age.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Children as young as five start training at one of our seven zone training centres that are located all across the island.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Students with good potential will start serious training from 10 years old and have an opportunity to be part of the Junior Development Squad, which has about 100 players.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Thereafter, at the secondary school level, about 40 players will be selected for the Youth Training Squad and School within Schools Programme.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: From this lot, between five and eight players will be selected for the Intermediate Squad.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And finally, the top 12 players will be selected into the National Team.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The fact is that less than 1% of the Zone Training Centre students will eventually make it into the National Team.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These youth players have many opportunities to compete locally and internationally.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many talented youths were discovered during the annual Crocodile Cup, Singapore Junior and Hopes International Tournament, Southeast Asia Junior and Asian Junior Table Tennis Championships and the World Table Tennis Youth Contender series.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In fact, most of our current National Team players started off as Crocodile Cup age-group champions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The outstanding players, with some as young as 12 years old, will get opportunities to compete in junior table tennis competitions overseas.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For instance, in April this year, 12-year-old Loy Ming Ying won her first under-13 gold medal in the World Table Tennis (WTT) Youth Contender held in Poland and her second gold medal in the under-13 WTT Youth Contender held in Berlin.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is extremely demanding for the youth players to cope with the challenges of having to achieve academically and, at the same time, to be able to perform during training.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To help them balance schoolwork with sports, the Singapore Sports School provides a flexible and athlete-centric academic approach around the athlete’s training and competition schedule.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: At the end of the day, athletes are still able to earn their diplomas and degrees while playing table tennis competitively.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Ten out of 13 national team players are alumni of the Singapore Sports School.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And medals and academic degrees are important but, in my view, the most valuable lesson from this rigorous youth development pathway will be the lessons on independence, resilience, discipline and teamwork.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There is a saying that it takes a village to raise a child.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In sports, it is a multi-million-dollar investment that takes years to groom a world-class champion.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The remaining expenses are self-funded by our training programmes and from goodwill donations from sponsors and donors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: STTA works closely with SportSG to map out multi-year sports plans and targets for international tournaments and major games.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To groom world-class players, they must consistently compete against the top players in the world or train with established table tennis leagues and academies.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We have signed memoranda of understanding (MOUs) with several table tennis academies in Europe and Asia so that players from both sides can train together and learn from each other.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The fact is that our paddlers are away from home most of the time as they travel to far-flung places across Africa, Latin America, Europe and Asia to compete, train or acclimatise well before major games.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We clearly spare no effort in providing maximum training and competition opportunities for our top players.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Over the past two years of intense competition and training stints, we have witnessed vast improvements in the technical skills and composure of our young national players, such as Izaac Quek, Koen Pang, Wong Xinru and Zhou Jingyi.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With each tournament, their world rankings improve so that they can qualify for major games and tournaments.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In the past, talented athletes would not have considered sports as a career.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Family members and friends would openly discourage them as it was truly difficult to survive as a professional athlete.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our times have since changed and there are signs that sports could now be considered as a viable career option.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With proper management, successful athletes, such as Joseph Schooling and Loh Kean Yew, were able to generate sizeable incomes from both prize monies as well as endorsement fees.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In addition, athletes who achieve podium finishes at the four major games will be rewarded with attractive prize monies from the SNOC Major Games Award Programme that is sponsored by the Tote Board Group.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In STTA, apart from the rewards, we will also prepare our national paddlers for eventual retirement.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The gratuity amount will correspond with the duration of their service, which can be drawn upon their retirement.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Most people may not be aware that beneath the glamour and fame of any recognised athlete, their schedule and expectations to achieve are extremely demanding.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To add, there is always a possibility that the athletes may suffer a serious injury and can no longer compete.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Professional sports can be very cruel because, after every victory, the athlete has to start from scratch again.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: If our national athletes are expected to devote their youth to sports and to go all out to win at competitions in order to fly our flag high, we have to assure parents that professional sports is a viable career.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our sporting ecosystem must be able to support the professional athletes not only while they are at their peak but also after their retirement.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is only fair that our athletes and their families have such an assurance.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Improvement is always necessary but identifying areas of improvement will be dependent on many factors, which include hidden challenges that may have absolutely nothing to do with sports, for example, issues like low birth rates and the relentless focus on academics.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Such are difficult issues that we will have to manage when evaluating not just Singapore’s sporting ecosystem but our economy as well.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Motion put forth by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Faisal Manap is a concern that is expressed in a very elemental manner.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Motion fails to identify any focus or highlight the sports or games that they were referring to.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Regardless of any Government participation to support any sports or games, achievement in sports requires an athlete’s passion, his desire to overcome obstacles to nurture a strong fighting spirit and a strong desire to achieve will always take precedence over any evaluation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Similarly, you can provide perks and have a goal like having our national soccer team participate in the World Cup finals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: When it is unrealistic, we must be able to admit that some goals are not quite possible to score yet.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The first clarification I have is for Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Chay, can you speak into the mic, please?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: The first clarification that I have is for Assoc Prof Jamus Lim on the nature of para sports and the economic considerations versus the performance that our para-athletes have in relation to national funding.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I am not an economics professor, but there are also positive externalities when it comes to having an economy that is doing well, in terms of healthcare, in terms of care for patients as well.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: So, I think that also speaks to the talent pool when we talk about the number of athletes representing our para-athlete contingent.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Second, I work with the Invictus Foundation, which is a foundation that enables war veterans to actually compete and still represent their countries even though they have been permanently injured as para-athletes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: And I think that Singapore is a relatively safe country.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: When it comes to the whole landscape of para-athletes, we also need to consider that because of our economic stability, safety, national defence, the pool of para-athletes is actually not very large.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: So, I would just like to ask Assoc Prof Jamus Lim if he has actually considered these in his comments.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Do you want to let Assoc Prof Jamus Lim —

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Do you have a second clarification for him?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I think I, at no point, suggested that our para-athletes were underperforming because we have a small population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If anything, I think the fact that our para-athletic team has done so well is something that we all feel extremely proud of.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Later on, I believe some of my Workers' Party colleagues will elaborate more on helping to further improve the diversity and inclusiveness of our sports scene, which includes the para-athletes' performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Again, I am not entirely clear what the specificity of the Member's quarrel with what I had said earlier was.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I think I might have misunderstood, but my clarification is on the rankings of the other Southeast Asia nations, as opposed to ours.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: And how our para-athletes have performed in terms of total medal tally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: That is how our para-athletes performed, and I can take the opportunity to clarify the earlier point that Ms Poh Li San said.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I am just wondering – so, your statements mean that —

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Mark Chay, can you address your clarifications to the Chair?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: This is actually the first time in two-and-a-half years that I am doing this.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Can you address your clarification to the Chair?

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, you can take your seat first.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: When it comes to sports, you cannot just look at the socio-economic background of a country specifically.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: You have to look at it as a whole.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I think that is the question that I had for Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, whether he considered it as a whole, not just looking at our economic status in the region.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And indeed, I emphasised in the speech that there were many elements, including the fact that we have a small population that does affect the relative performance of our national teams, whether in terms of the SEA Games or the Para Games.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But if anything, socio-economic status tends to drive a great deal of the performance outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And in that regard specifically, it is clear to me, at least based on the data, that we massively underperformed.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Actually, I do have another clarification for the Leader of the House pertaining to his comments about —

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Do you mean the Leader of the Opposition?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I think we have clarified this in the House before that the swimmers admitted to the consumption of marijuana.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: There was no criminal act of proceedings or infringements here.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: So, I just wanted to clarify that and ask if he is aware of that as well.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Also, SNOC called the disciplinary committee (DC) for the swimmers.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: They paid a fine and this was all done before the selection for the SEA Games.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: While I note the points he is making, they do not detract from the larger point vis-à-vis those two issues which I raised, which was that SNOC has a track record of looking and displaying a forgiving attitude towards athletes who may have committed transgressions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think that is the key point, which I hope SNOC and the Ministry also can take into account for other athletes who may have fallen short.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Yes, indeed, SNOC has – and I have to declare that I am not a member of SNOC.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: But I was on the Selection Committee in 2021 when we decided not to send Soh Rui Yong for various reasons.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: But I do want to say that these athletes have had their disciplinary committees, they have already served their penalties.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: They were sorry and we have all moved on.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: So, SNOC does have that track record of that.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: He seemed very sorry for what he had done.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: There was also a commitment from him to — I am not going to go into the details of the commitment.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Well, with respect to the commitment, he said that he would not make disparaging comments and he would abide by the Code of Conduct, that he was sorry.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: He went to the SEA Games – well and good, right?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: So, he did participate in the SEA Games.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: So, that was the result of his non-selection in the Asian Games in 2023.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I would also like to say that this is not uncommon in the world.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I believe that Singapore Athletics believes that he still abides by the Code of Conduct and they still select him and nominate him for these games.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: So, he can still compete, he can still break national records, but not at the major games.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Where leniency was given, he took advantage of the situation.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: And that is why he was not selected for the Asian Games.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think I have mentioned a few times in my speech and I was careful to do it to restate that it is important for athletes to abide by standards of discipline.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I am appealing also as his Member of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And if SNOC can take another look at him, I am not out of order, I believe, to raise this matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And – given that the matter actually goes far beyond, in the eyes of many, just to be an issue of transgressions – I hope more senior members of our sporting fraternity can come in and try to lower temperatures, so that athletes like Soh Rui Yong can participate and fly the flag proudly.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Sorry, Madam, I just have one more clarification for Mr Leon Perera.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I have just one clarification on the support for athletes who are not in popular sports.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: He cited bowling as well as billiards, with Peter Gilchrist, Aloysius Yapp, Shayna Ng as well as Cherie Tan.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: SportSG actually does give them funding and support, both in sports science as well as grants.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: So, I just wanted to understand whether he is aware that spexScholarship does exist for athletes in this situation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I did, in my speech, allude to my awareness of the existence of sports scholarships and I mentioned a few, nor in my speech did I claim that there is no Government support for these less well-known sports.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In fact, I highlighted, in the case of cue sports, the Government funding that is given to them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My point for the part of my speech about less well-known sports is that we do have top performers in some of these sports.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It is not very widely known or well-known, and there is room to do more, in terms of trying to understand why they have succeeded, unpacking the reasons, replicating the factors and ecosystem and building on that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And I would like to ask the hon Member Mr Chay if he feels that there is no room for improvement in terms of the support – whether as a Government, as a society, the NSAs or SportSG – given to less well-known sports.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Does he feel that there is absolutely no room for improvement at all?

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Perera, in future, please direct it to the Chair.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Yes, I do think that there is room for improvement and there is definitely no perfect system.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: There are a lot of wonderful systems out there, but we have got to do the right system for what works in Singapore, and we have success in the systems that we have right now.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Obviously, we need to continually improve on them.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Yes, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we definitely need to continue to improve on them and support our athletes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: But based on the systems that we have today, they are working.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I am not saying that they are perfect.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: There is always room for improvement and I think that is part of why we are debating this Motion today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I wonder if the hon Member was paying attention to Assoc Prof Jamus Lim when he presented the data.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Please speak into the microphone, I cannot hear you.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I acknowledge that, of course, no system is perfect.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Would the hon Member recognise that or does he feel that the data is wrong or he feels that it is not appropriate to make that comparison, to analyse the data in that way?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I recognise the hon Member's comments and I recognise that there was a fancy chart with GDP, but we cannot look at athlete performance juxtaposed to GDP alone.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I was a Primary 5 kid, a basket kid, taking the track suits out.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: We have achieved so much in the past 50, 60 years.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: The other systems need time to catch up and I think we should view this as well in the analysis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just a very quick clarification for the Member.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Does he feel that we should exercise exactly the same modicum of patience with all the other areas that Singapore rightly excels in on the international stage?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Whether we are happy that we have taken 20 years and, if anything, we have fallen much further away in terms of the relative performance of our football team, even as we have gotten relatively richer?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: Definitely for sports, I say we need to take a measured approach where we are very young in this whole idea of sports administration and high performance.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: We started building our facilities back in 1960s and 1970s only.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: We were playing football on the Padang and Farrer Park.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: You are looking at the Secondary 1, Secondary 2 kids today and they take time to mature.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: So, we may have the facilities here, but you still need to continue to grow and groom these kids to be able to give them appropriate level competitions in order to produce results in 10 years' time.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: That is just my view – you cannot expect the results to come immediately, especially when you talk about high performance, dynamic sports like football.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I do not claim to be an expert but when you are dealing with 11 men on one team and 11 men on the other team, a lot of things can happen.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I used to be the CEO of Singapore Hockey Federation.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: I can tell you that team sport is extremely complex.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: It is not like individual sports, where it is one person on the track, seven in a single lane.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay
text: You have to talk about having everyone performing in sync, in concert, together.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: You could have the auntie doing tai-chi daily in the park to the 30-something weekend warrior battling away with his football buddies to the elite athletes who undergo the gruelling training in the pursuit of their Olympian goal.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sporting success would thus be different things to different people.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should thus not define sporting success only by medals won or quantitative targets attained.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just as sports and sporting activities can play multiple roles in our community, such as fostering national pride and connecting or bonding people from all walks of life, we should also measure sporting success by looking at whether or not these broader goals have been met or attained via sports.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In short, let us not be too narrow in defining sporting success.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As an educator of more than 20 years, I have always believed in the value of a holistic education, and sports and sporting activity are a key part of a holistic education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It helps shape a person's beliefs and attitude towards overcoming challenges in life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Athletes undergo gruelling challenges in their sporting pursuits.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through these, he picks up the skills that are valuable to the corporate world.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some skills our athletes might pick up include: resilience, the ability to bounce back from failure; fortitude, the strength to keep going when the going gets tough; humility, the ability to embrace critical feedback in their continuous journey of self-improvement; and also cooperation and empathy, especially for those involved in team sports.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that many corporate partners recognise this and do step forward to support our athletes in their professional life beyond sports, and this is critical as the shelf life of a professional athlete is relatively short compared to many other professions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand that it has been 10 years since the Government set up the spexBusiness Network.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened that Athlete Life Management is a key area of focus for SSI and the National Youth Sports Institute (NYSI).

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is about integrating sports performance with key aspects of an athlete’s life and total well-being, including mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And like in education, supporting our athletes’ total well-being is an effort requiring partnership across multiple stakeholders – coaches, psychologists, National Sports Associations (NSAs) and even parents.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My daughter is an active junior competitive swimmer.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: She is 11-plus, but, as a parent, I have already seen the kind of stresses and pressure that competitive athletes at that level go through – training six times a week, two hours per session, more than 50-60 laps each time in the pool at six in the morning, juggling their homework and so on.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I am truly heartened and am a big advocate of making sure that we have that mental and emotional wellness support for our athletes as well, both young and the not-so-young.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ahead of major competitions, I understand SSI and NYSI assign Sport Psychologists and Athlete Life personnel to provide more dedicated psychological and mental well-being support for our national athletes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This support includes one-on-one consultations and imparting skills to athletes to manage their mental and emotional conditions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Support, Mdm Deputy Speaker, needs to go beyond major competitions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should equip coaches and relevant personnel like sports administrators with the skills needed to proactively identify and support athletes who may be experiencing issues with their mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They should also be able to refer athletes to appropriate sources of help.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should also work with the respective NSAs to build the mental resilience of our athletes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the body responsible for grooming Team Singapore athletes for their sport, the NSAs play an important role to help our athletes develop coping mechanisms and ways to practise self-care.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, I hope that mental and emotional wellness support and help can be made available even after athletes have retired from the competitive arena.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although not at the illustrious levels of our Olympian colleague Mr Mark Chay or even at the levels of former national sportsman Deputy Speaker Christopher de Souza, I have always played a variety of sports at a fairly competitive level.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And my daughter, as I mentioned earlier, is continuing that family tradition as a competitive junior swimmer.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also began my professional career in sports broadcasting 30 years ago as a TV presenter for the 1993 SEA Games.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And that was the SEA Games held in Singapore after almost 20 years, if Members recall.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have also noted some comments from my other Parliamentary colleagues along these lines.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And Ms Poh also alluded to the proactive approach towards a sporting ecosystem and how regular reviews are institutionalised as part and parcel of the NSAs’ partnership with SportSG.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Can I have a copy of your amendment?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Could I have the assistance of the Clerks to distribute the copies, if Madam gives the go-ahead?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: So, we ought to recognise their accomplishments at other major competitions, not just the Asian Games, ASEAN Para Games, Olympics and Paralympics, but also single-sport competitions at the regional and world levels, which are, really, what we have been talking about.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Many Members here have been talking about many other sports, beyond the traditional sports and many competitions even, beyond the Olympics, Paralympics, Asian Games, SEA Games and so on.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Regular reviews of policies and goals are a key feature of our system.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: So, I would like to propose that we continue all these reviews and all these assessments for the overall benefit of our sporting ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: The final point is in relation to deleting "clear, achievable goals for sporting success" and inserting "our goals in sports".

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: I think success should be measured beyond just that one particular quantitative marker.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Also, our broader objectives of sports are to help athletes reach their maximum potential and also to broaden participation in sports, rally our communities, foster national pride and cohesion, or even just about being the best version of yourself that you can be.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: As I tell my daughter, it is not about winning the medals, it is about improving your personal best every time you go into the pool.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: All of us, we have got to have that personal best – amateur sportsmen, professional sportsmen – and I believe that we should, therefore, proceed along these lines.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Do I have the hon Members' agreement to this?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On behalf of the Progress Singapore Party (PSP), I would, first, like to offer my congratulations to TeamSG's athletes and para-athletes for their achievements at the 32nd Southeast Asian Games and the 12th ASEAN Para Games in Cambodia.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our athletes and para-athletes have done themselves, their families and their country proud.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We call on the Government to continue to review Singapore's sporting ecosystem and identify opportunity areas where we can provide more support to help our nation and our athletes achieve greater success in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have two areas of review to suggest.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While this has been extensively covered by the Leader of the Opposition and clarified further by Mr Mark Chay, however, please allow me to speak up one more time for Soh Rui Yong.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the recent SEA Games, Soh Rui Yong has once again shown that he is a talented and record-setting runner.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He has demonstrated the potential to continue bringing glory to Singapore at the Asian Games.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, he cannot do so because he has supposedly not met the SNOC's selection criteria, which encompass athletes' attitudes, behaviours, general conduct and disciplinary history.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More clarity is needed around the process by which an athlete is disqualified from representing Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP also believes that all sports associations should be led by people with professional expertise and interest in the sport.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will ensure that Singapore's sporting ecosystem is driven by athletes who know how to succeed in the sport and are committed to have the sport succeed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such leaders will be more likely to understand the needs of our professional athletes and be able to work with them to advance Singapore's international standing in these sports.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another area where we can provide greater support to athletes as a nation is greater flexibility around National Service (NS) obligations, which I have spoken on last August.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would make a great difference to the sporting careers of our male athletes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last year, our Olympic gold medallist Joseph Schooling called for a national dialogue on managing expectations of athletes undergoing National Service.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He related to the media the challenges of serving NS and trying to excel in the pool at the same time and the expectations from the public to perform.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2018 and 2022, the Minister for Defence explained Singapore's deferment policies in this House, which are grounded on the principles of national security, universality and equity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These principles mean that every Singaporean must serve NS at the time he is required to do under the Enlistment Act.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, in recent years, there are many Singaporeans who are concerned that many male foreigners are given citizenship without having to serve NS while our male sports talents miss out on the opportunity to develop their sporting careers because they must serve NS.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The policies around such deferments should be determined through a national dialogue around NS deferments.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe it is timely to have such a dialogue to discuss how the criteria for such deferments can support our young male athletes in achieving sporting success while still being explicit, transparent and fair and satisfy the principles of national security, universality and equity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These include Aljunied GRC residents, Kimberly Ong, Colin Soon, Sophie Soon and Soh Rui Yong.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: You have done your family, the sports fraternity and your country proud by flying the Singapore flag high on the world stage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I also wish all our Asian Games athletes and para-athletes the best of success in their preparations and competitions at the upcoming Asian Games and Asian Para Games in October.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My speech today will focus on the development of high-performance athletes in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I will delve into some of the challenges faced in the local sports ecosystem and will propose several ideas that I believe will enable Singapore to achieve greater success in the international sporting arena.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Before I continue, I wish to declare my interest in this matter as a parent with a child who trains in a high-performance sports programme supported by SportSG.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most of us would be familiar with the 10,000-hour rule.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a concept proposed by Dr Anders Ericsson and popularised by Malcolm Gladwell in his 2008 book, Outliers: The Story of Success.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The rule suggests that it takes approximately 10,000 hours of deliberate practice to achieve mastery in a particular field or skill.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To clock 10,000 hours, an athlete would need to put in three hours a day of practice six days a week, continuously, for over 10 years.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Going by this rule, if an athlete aims to be world-class by the age of 18, they would need to start serious training when they are just eight years old.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This does not even take into account the quality of their training and their innate talent, which are important factors for their future success.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, many world-class athletes today started training in the high-performance environment from as young an age as five.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many were handpicked while they were still learning to walk, often by their own parents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In his autobiography, "Black and White", Richard Williams describes how he came up with the plan to train his two daughters to become tennis champions before they were even born.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We all know how successful Venus and Serena Williams became.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There are also many other instances of fraught relationships between parents and their child athletes, even to the point of abuse.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And I am not suggesting that Richard Williams' approach is right for every athlete.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, this is the nature of an international competition young athletes are up against.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For most sports, in order to become a world-class athlete, the period of very high intensity training often starts from the age of 12 or even younger.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This coincides with the time Singaporean students are the busiest, preparing for their PSLE, "O" and "A" levels.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Training for just a few hours a week with the school's co-curricular activity (CCA) sports team is not high-performance training and this pace of training will generally limit the students' success in their sport to inter-school sports competitions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is extremely challenging for a secondary school student in a mainstream local school to balance this heavy load of training, travel and competition with their studies without burning themselves out physically, mentally and emotionally.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: An exception is found in the Singapore Sports School where academic schedules are customised to accommodate the student athletes' training and competition commitments.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The hon Member Poh Li San shared about this earlier, too.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Sports School has produced some very successful graduates, including badminton player Loh Kean Yew and table tennis player Clarence Chew, who have both won gold for our nation at international competitions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This leads me to my next point: the Singaporean outlook towards the nexus of sports and studies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore, the well-established route for young individuals to achieve a comfortable income and provide for their family involved completing their education, graduating from either a polytechnic or university and securing a professional position, preferably in a bank, tech company or law firm.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Becoming a professional athlete, on the other hand, is probably one of the most difficult paths a Singaporean can choose.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is not a ticket out of poverty in Singapore as it is in some countries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Those outside these rankings may struggle to even cover their expenses, which include travel, accommodation, coaching and physiotherapy fees.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In lower-paying sports, athletes must depend on salaries paid by their clubs or NSAs to cover their expenses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Despite the desire for sports champions in Singapore, pragmatism often leads parents to view pursuing a professional sports career as impractical for their children.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Consequently, many talented student athletes choose to enter top mainstream secondary schools through the Direct School Admission programme rather than attending the specialised Singapore Sports School.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is despite the fact that the latter often offers a more favourable environment for balancing both sports and studies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, student athletes enrol in mainstream schools encounter constraints when compared to their peers in the Sports School.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The fixed timetables in mainstream schools do not cater specifically to athletes, making it difficult for them to undergo long hours of training and overseas competition.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While some mainstream schools offer limited flexibility on an individual basis, such as permitting athletes to skip a week of school for international competitions, the time away from lessons eventually takes a toll on their studies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With this reality in play, we should not be surprised that we continue to have a narrow pipeline of world-class athletes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The "academics-first" approach is one that most Singaporeans have chosen over the years and will continue to choose in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given that many high-performance athletes are of school-going age, if nothing is done to shift the youth sports development paradigm, we will continue to see many budding sports stars eventually fizzle out after they complete secondary school.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, given how important academics are to Singaporeans, it is not fruitful to try to persuade them to choose sports over studies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should, therefore, explore pathways that allow student athletes to pursue both their studies and sports at the highest level.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is possible through what is known as the college pathway.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most universities in the United States are members of the National Collegiate Athletic Association, or NCAA.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The top tier, known as Division I, runs inter-collegiate championships in 13 male and 13 female sports, including swimming, soccer, track and field, tennis, golf, water polo, field hockey, basketball, volleyball and diving.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many of these are popular sports in Singapore which our athletes compete in during major games, like the SEA Games, Asian Games and the Olympics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: College sports is huge in the US and has a television audience comparable to the top professional team sports.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This popularity attracts commercial sponsors and television licensing rights and is a huge revenue earner for some universities to the tune of some US$30 million a year.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The quality of college sports in the US is so high that many of the best junior athletes from all over the world, including Europe, Australia and China, vie for the opportunity to study in these universities on full athletics scholarships while competing in their sport.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many of these universities have students that win more international championships than many small nations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many of the top performing universities in inter-collegiate sports are also top-ranked academic institutions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They include Stanford UC Berkeley, Duke University of Michigan, UCLA and USC.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Harvard, Princeton, UPenn and other Ivy League universities are also NCAA Division I members.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the Ivy league is a Collegiate Athletic Conference comprising eight schools in northeastern US, although it is more commonly used to refer to academically elite American universities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By pursuing the college pathway, more Singaporean student athletes can have the opportunity to benefit from the best of both worlds, a top-quality university education and elite level competition in their sport.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: College sports can be a springboard to the professional leagues after graduation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Several Singaporeans who competed for US colleges returned to represent Singapore in major games.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These include swimmer Joseph Schooling who graduated from the University of Texas at Austin; golfer Hailey Loh, who is studying in California Baptist University and our Parliamentary colleague, the hon Member Mark Chay, who graduated from Brigham Young University.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even those who do not ultimately make it into an American university, the disciplined focus in both academics and sports through the secondary school years will better prepare student athletes to enter our local polytechnics and universities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Athletes are also much sought after by many companies after they graduate because many employers recognise that athletes' discipline, drive and good time management skills are among the many valuable skills that they bring to the workplace.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Despite the attractiveness of the college pathway, there appears to be a lack of awareness about it among many student athletes and their parents about the steps they need to take to pursue it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: SportSG, NSAs, sports academies, schools and coaches should conduct more sharing sessions and provide more guidance for athletes and their parents on the college pathway.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will allow parents and athletes to make considered plans in developing their proficiency in their sport.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The college pathway could provide a stronger pipeline of athletes in several sports that Singapore has potential to excel in, at major games.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My second suggestion is that the Singapore Sports School should expand its enrolment of students beyond the nine "academy sports" and provide a study-and-train environment for more student athletes who can demonstrate their interest and potential to compete at an international level in their sport.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To make this successful, the Sports School and SportSG need to better market the benefits of their sports and academic programmes to prospective students.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Sports School can arrange more sharing sessions at various primary schools nationwide, in addition to the existing Sports School open house.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It could also invite the high-performing athletes in primary schools for holiday camps at the Sports School during the school holidays.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These will enable the young athletes and parents to better understand and familiarise themselves with the Sports School.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Sports School will then be able to better attract a critical mass of students in each sport that will, in turn, make the school more attractive to prospective students.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Third, despite interest in sports, the local media should play a bigger role in featuring local athletes in international competitions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When Singaporeans turn on their television sets to watch sports, they seldom see their compatriots competing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, it is so rare to see Singaporeans in world-class sports competitions that when it does happen, like when Loh Kean Yew won the badminton world championships in 2021, many of us specifically tuned in to watch them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Unfortunately, in the case of Loh Kean Yew's amazing win, it was so unexpected that even our public broadcaster did not make preparations to broadcast the final match live to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There should not just be a daily highlights programme which features a few athletes in action.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The media features could include interviews with high-performance athletes sharing their insights about their day-to-day schedules and training.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: All these will spark interest in the various sports among athletes, fans and commercial sponsors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My fourth and final suggestion is to parents of athletes and the athletes themselves.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Parents have an out-sized influence on their children's sporting ambitions and progress, from a very young age through their growing years.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I say this as a reminder to myself, too.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most athletes will only have the intrinsic motivation to push themselves to reach the pinnacle of their arena if they genuinely enjoy participating in the sport.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Your child must know that you love them, regardless of their results on the field.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The path will be less well-trodden than the ones most of their peers are taking and there is no guarantee of success.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is, therefore, important to focus on enjoying the journey, not just the destination.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When Singaporeans cheer in support of our sportsmen and women, listen to Majulah Singapura playing at the podium or see Singaporean athletes giving their all on the field, in the pool or on the court, we all feel an immense rush of pride in our nation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, for a nation as wealthy and as diverse as Singapore, our record of performance in sports on the world stage leaves much to be desired.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have outlined four suggestions aimed at improving Singapore's sporting ecosystem to build a stronger and more sustainable pipeline of high-performance athletes in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will help us take steps towards realising our goals for sporting success over the coming decades and for many decades to come.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I strongly support the Motion standing in the names of my hon friends Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Muhamad Faisal Abdul Manap.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My speech will cover the following four points: first, I support the Motion where we acknowledge the hard work by our athletes and our para-athletes; second, I will highlight why broad-based accessible programming to encourage more people to participate in sports is key in building up our talent pool for high-performance sports; third, I will speak on the need to ensure inclusivity through sports; and fourth, as a lifelong football fan, I hope to offer some suggestions for Singapore's football to, once again, reach the heights of the 1980s and 1990s.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While news about our best-performing athletes and para-athletes, especially those who have consecutively broken records, might dominate news headlines and deservedly generate the most hype, we must also not forget the rest of our athletes who did not win medals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Every athlete trains hard and they sacrifice their time with family and friends with every intention of doing their best for themselves and for the country they represent.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They were not in the competitions just to make up the numbers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The amended Motion, therefore, acknowledges the hard work, blood, sweat and tears of our TeamSG athletes, both past and present.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Broad-based accessible programming that encourages sports participation will be a key part of this approach, as we need a broad participation base from which we can identify and develop sporting talent.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I personally know how challenging it is to organise such sporting programmes and keep the participation strong.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Years ago, in 2011, I started the Delta League programme.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is now a bi-annual youth engagement programme that aims to engage youths through football and keep them meaningfully occupied during the long June and December school holidays.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Jointly organised by the Police and the National Crime Prevention Council (NCPC), there are also talks and activities besides the football clinics and matches that inculcate in our youths a sense of social responsibility, teamwork and discipline.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Delta League programme complements several other programmes in our community, including the SportCares initiatives by SportSG.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Every year, SportSG also partners different sports organisations to bring about Pesta Sukan.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is the largest multi-sports competition in Singapore designed for the community.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The categories of the different sports range from Open, Masters, Youth, Community and Corporate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: There are also other sporting activities, such as the Stadium Run and SG Urban Walk Challenge.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Basically, my point is that there is a sporting activity for everyone.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is important to have events like these to encourage everyone to come together to play sports, regardless of age, ability and background.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With more people participating in sports, we can not only have a wider pool to identify sporting talents who can go on to do us proud on the world podium but also cultivate a nation of people who can better appreciate sports, which goes a long way to growing our sporting nation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I, therefore, encourage Members of the House to rally your own constituents to participate in the Pesta Sukan activities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We can all join in as participants, as spectators or simply to cheer on our friends and family.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lastly, let me move on to a sport that has a special place in my heart and, I believe, in the hearts of many Singaporeans – football.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Members will agree with me that it is evident that our football scene requires a lot of work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I note that the Football Association of Singapore (FAS) has commissioned a panel to conduct a review of the team’s performances and will share their findings and recommendations soon.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would, nonetheless, like to give some suggestions on how we can improve the state of our football.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I start with our lack of dedicated infrastructure and facilities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Unlike some of our neighbouring countries, we have limited training grounds and stadiums equipped with quality football facilities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, as some Members have already highlighted, we cannot even play football at our void decks and many of our neighbourhood school football fields and parks have restricted use.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This scarcity restricts the number of local talents that can be groomed and inhibits the organising of more football events and competitions, which then limits the exposure that our players receive.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Hence, it is vital for us to invest in the development of infrastructure to provide our athletes with the necessary ecosystem of support and opportunities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Next, we must improve the way we groom our pipeline of football talents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We need to establish a robust talent scouting and recruitment system to identify early promising players.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Only by identifying them early when they are young and by continuously nurturing them can Singapore build a strong pool of players who can contribute to the national team and compete internationally.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One of the best ways I found in scouting our talents is to search from the grassroots, and the Delta League is one good example.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And over the years, some of them have been scouted to play at club level and, eventually, some have gone on to train with the national teams.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And I welcome the FAS scouts to attend our Delta League matches.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Exposing our local players to different playing styles and allowing them to benchmark their abilities against international competitors can help them better develop their own skills and broaden their knowledge of the game.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I, therefore, support the amended Motion as proposed by the hon Member Darryl David.
