text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.30 pm.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 5.09 pm until 5.30 pm.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I believe that sporting success, as the original Motion calls for, should not only be measured in terms of winning medals and doing well in various rankings, but also measured in terms of wider participation in sports across all segments of society.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Specifically, I will talk about how we do on accessibility and participation in sports and how this measurement should form an important part of our national developmental dashboard, an idea I first raised in Parliament in early 2022.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I will also touch on inclusion in sports, from how we provide for the mental well-being of our athletes, to the crucial and important role that sports play to work with and support persons with disabilities and also neurodiverse individuals.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is clearly an achievement worth celebrating and I hope that this can be maintained.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Two, sports are instrumental to many other things we see as important to our well-being, including our physical and mental health, and play an important role in other national priorities, including fostering national cohesion and the creation of sustainable good jobs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As my WP colleagues have spoken about participation in sports at the top levels, I would like to share some observations about more general participation in sports in our daily life, which I believe should be a key part of our measurement of sporting success.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Besides the obvious benefits outlined above, I believe participation in sports at any level can teach us many life lessons that will stand us in good stead as we go along our path in life.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I was, for most of my early years, fairly bookish and sedentary and did not particularly enjoy any type of physical activity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, this changed at university, when I was persuaded by friends to attend a football training session for our college one weekend in my first week.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Still a little homesick and coming to terms with a new life in a foreign land miles from home, and despite never having watched the game beyond clips of highlights occasionally on TV as I was growing up, my curiosity got the better of me.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It was to be the start of my three-year journey with what eventually became known as the Corpus Terriers, as we cobbled together a ragtag group of students – both undergraduates and postgraduates – to become a good enough team that progressed from the bottom league, to gaining promotion twice to the league above in the university league tables.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: By my second year, I was having such fun being part of the football team that I doubled down and agreed to also join the college rowing team and was part of the first eight that year.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What participation in these sports taught me was not about winning or losing, but about the importance of perseverance and being there for your teammates.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It did not matter if you were out in a nightclub or panic writing an essay until three in the morning the night before.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Come 6.30 the next morning, whatever the weather, you were expected to be there on the river, ready to start training, or else you would be the reason the rest of the team was unable to go out on the water.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I have many memories of having to row on with ice forming on our blades, of beautiful winter sunrises seen on the river and of having to play on in horrible winter drizzle, rain and mud, and of having to swap the footballs midway through a match to fluorescent snow-balls in order to be able to see through the fog.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The time we spent together as friends, as a team, on the river and the playing fields, more than the hours spent trying to make sense of dense and opaque scientific journal articles, is what I remember when I think of my time at university almost two decades on.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They also gave us important lessons in grit, resilience, risk-taking and the importance of having one another's backs – skills that ring through across so many areas of life long after leaving the formal education system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It also teaches us how to deal with often very strong negative emotions in a healthy manner.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Experiencing first-hand the physical and mental health benefits of participating in sports made it easier for me to make a conscious effort to carve out time and to seek out suitable sporting activities to fit my current circumstances despite busy work and family schedules, especially here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What these experiences taught me is that we need to work to ensure that all of us – no matter who or where we are in life – are able to understand the benefits of sports – particularly organised sports – and reap these benefits.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Starting from our very young, we have to continue to work to make sports and physical activity fun for all children and find ways to sustainably incorporate it into daily life in a way that complements and not competes with academic learning.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It can be as simple as stopping ourselves from shouting at our young children to stop when they have a sudden impulse to run or jump, but instead pause and ask them how they can run or jump in a manner that is both safe and situationally appropriate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As our children grow up, the sporting ecosystem has to evolve to be supportive and accessible enough to allow them to choose a sport they enjoy and have an interest in, at a level of participation they are comfortable with and that fits into their current life circumstances.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And while we are on the topic of participation, we also must not neglect the important role of our participation in sports as spectators.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the National Sport Participation Survey (NSPS) found that there appeared to be high levels of positive responses associated with a sense of national pride in our achievements in sports, how does this translate into attendance at live sporting events?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, any competitive athlete will tell you that competing live is a truly unique and irreplaceable experience, and that the roar of the crowd is often instrumental in their performance during the match or race, and home support can make the difference between victory or defeat.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, this seems to be an area which we struggle with.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is also a contrast against the huge queues with fans camping overnight for tickets to matches, which even resulted in a tragic stampede in 1977 which resulted in casualties and even a life lost.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Contrast sports event attendance, too, to the fans who flooded the Internet and even started camping from yesterday for tickets for when Taylor Swift will play at the National Stadium next year.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Lack of spectator participation also was an issue when I assisted to organise an international wheelchair Rugby Fours tournament held at Toa Payoh Sports Hall and the Singapore Cricket Club, which was attended by teams from Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Australia and Europe.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Despite the skilled havoc on the court in play – making for a wonderful spectator experience – we struggled to get more than a handful of spectators to attend the matches in Toa Payoh.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This was a point made by Rohit Brijnath, The Straits Times assistant sports editor, who compared this against the 300 to 400 fans who turned up in an earlier leg of the tournament in Palembang.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It was a shame, particularly as the Singapore team comprised members with incredible stories that I believe would have been very inspirational to people who actually watched them play.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My kids certainly still remember sitting in the stands and watching the matches and talk about it periodically, even today.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Apart from the benefits I outlined earlier, exposure to sports, whether as spectators or otherwise, also exposes us to intangible lessons in terms of the culture surrounding various sports, such as the importance of focus and balance in tai chi and yoga, the importance of harmony in aikido, and the respect for the opponents in a sport like kendo, where participants do not celebrate scoring a point out of respect for your opponent who has after all trained as hard as you have.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Moving on to sporting success for people with disabilities, I am glad that we recognise its importance and that new initiatives continue to be launched, such as the Para Sport Academy last year and the move to make all ActiveSG gyms more inclusive by 2026.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While I appreciate the need to develop specific hard infrastructure for people with disabilities to participate in some sports, we must put a lot more effort into growing broad, regular participation in sports for them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But the definition of the sports participation rate indicator only tracks whether an individual has participated in any sports or recreational physical activities in the past year.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This definition is also different from the one used for the wider population in the National Sport Participation Survey (NSPS), which uses the headline definition of regular participation of at least once a week.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It would be good to harmonise the indicators used to better understand where we stand.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Particularly for running, walking and wheelchair use, cycle and walk paths often do not actually meet the Government's walking and cycling design guide specifications, despite these specifications already making large allowances for our urban density.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There often does not seem to have any safe passing distance designed for walking and cycling paths for those with disabilities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, intra-town cycling paths can be designed to be just two metres in width.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The guidelines also allow for designs encouraging footpath users to enter cycling paths to manoeuvre away from oncoming cyclists or pedestrians in cases where footpaths and cycling paths are next to each other, including in the case of wheelchair users.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Running, walking and wheelchair use are among the most popular and lowest barrier to entry sports for people with disabilities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To get the basic building blocks for disability sports, we must first get everyday active mobility design right.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Member for Aljunied GRC, Mr Leon Perera, also spoke earlier about lesser-known or less popular sports, and I note that this issue is even more pertinent for PWDs' participation in less popular sports.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many of us in this House lauded the achievements and success of our paralympians and, in particular, our para-equestrian athletes, such as Laurentia Tan, who was the first Asian woman to win a Paralympic medal in equestrian sport in Beijing 2008.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is of note that para-equestrian events have their roots in therapy riding.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And equine-assisted therapy is widely known to have myriad benefits, ranging from benefiting mental health and well-being, to therapeutic horseback riding, all of which work to build core muscles, balance, confidence, sensory motor skills and are also extremely calming and relational.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And these benefits accrue, too, to typical and non-disabled individuals.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, in spite of this, only a small handful of Singaporeans have access to equine-related sports and therapy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Uncertainty over whether the lease will be renewed or if the stables will continue to be allowed to operate only adds to the stresses that they face.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Horses aside, I also hope that, more generally, we also need to start paying more attention to accommodations that sporting participation – both as sportspeople and spectators – can make to cater to more diversity, particularly neurodiversity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, individuals with sensory sensitivities or on the autism spectrum may find taking part in organised sports difficult to cope with because of the sensory input or unmet expectations, and I hope that parents and officials are given the right awareness and tools to know how best to cope with unexpected situations that arise.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This could take the form of training officials and coaches to communicate more effectively with these individuals, to better awareness for parents about which sports may suit their child's specific needs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also note that exhibits at places like KidsSTOP at the Science Centre have labels that stipulate sensory levels for various exhibits to aid parents to know whether the exhibit is suitable for their child, and perhaps the same system can be applied in the sporting context.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Far from resulting in the "wussification" of our top athletes, I note that greats from previous eras, such as Billie Jean King, have been equally outspoken about their concerns on this and do good work to increase awareness and support for current top athletes operating and competing in a brutal environment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In turn, spectators and sports fans alike should also be aware of how we ventilate our frustrations when our team or our favourite athletes suffer defeats or setbacks, as seen from the wave of anger and abuse our Lions team and Joseph Schooling, for example, received online in recent times after painful losses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Despite our disappointment, we must remember to continue standing behind our teams and athletes through thick and thin.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also hope that our sports training programmes with the National Youth Sports Institute and other sports associations adequately prepare our often extremely young athletes for life as a professional athlete, which should go beyond how to cope on the pitch but also off the pitch, not just mental health and well-being but also in navigating media exposure and pressures online and off, and even making appropriate decisions over sponsorship and funding options.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our agencies need to focus more on the fundamental issues that improve access and participation for all, especially persons with disabilities and different needs, which include ensuring our urban mobility standards are improved and followed properly by developers to help us keep on the path towards our aspirations with sports, as well as help us reap the significant social, economic and health benefits of becoming a sporting nation for all.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I support the Motion put forward by Sengkang GRC Member Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Aljunied GRC Member Mr Faisal Manap.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I was inspired by the athletes I watched in international competitions, pushing themselves beyond the limits of physical and mental boundaries, determined to fly their national flags high.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am often left in awe, in the wake of sporting excellence – from Olympic gymnast Nadia Comaneci scoring perfect 10s in 1976 in Montreal, to earlier heroes like Emil Zatopek, who won the 5,000 metres, 10,000 metres and marathon in the same Olympic Games in Helsinki in 1952, to our very own champions C Kunalan and Chee Swee Lee, to our Malaysia Cup winners playing the beautiful game.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For me, sporting excellence was and still is a pure form of sincerity and commitment to the nation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Putting it lyrically, it is poetry in motion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The pinnacle of my achievement was winning the ladies' section of the National University of Singapore's (NUS) mini-triathlon in my final year of undergraduate studies and, later, some cross-country runs in organisations that I worked for.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, modest as my endeavours were, I paid a physical price.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I aggravated a hip problem and sustained cartilage tears which plagued my quality of life as I entered my 40s and 50s.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I stopped running, switched to modified and low impact activities like swimming and focused on recovery and strength building in order to age well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I share this experience to illustrate what is but a fraction of what our national athletes do to their bodies, over and over again, at higher intensities and on a much larger scale.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The intensity and consistency one needs to put in to represent Singapore at global competitions, facing off against the best in the region and the world, is beyond imagination.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Top athletes, such as golfing legend Tiger Woods and basketball sensation Yao Ming, had their sporting careers prematurely ended or cut short by injury.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The mental pressure is another aspect which we are still learning more about, thanks to the likes of Japanese tennis star, Osaka Naomi.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for sports-related physical injuries, they can persist for a long time, both in recreational and competitive athletes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A recent Straits Times article found that youths have been suffering from sports-related injuries in the post-pandemic period at a higher rate and that injuries sustained in youth are likely to recur in some form later in life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Frequent or severe sports injuries may also put youths at risk of longer-term wear-and-tear-related degenerative conditions, such as osteoarthritis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Orthopaedic surgeon Dr Tan Ken Jin shared his observations in a 2022 article entitled "10 Sports Injuries with Lifelong Consequences".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The 10 lifelong sports injuries he pinpointed were sprains, hamstring strains, stress fractures, anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries, patella or kneecap dislocations, meniscus tears, tennis elbow, shoulder dislocations, sciatica or lower back pain and fractures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These injuries could have resulted from improper training practices, wearing improper sporting gear or basic elements like not having proper warm-ups or stretching.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even with all these things done properly, getting injured is commonplace in competitive sports, particularly in high impact sports, such as basketball, soccer, badminton, tennis, volleyball, hockey and gymnastics.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The injuries do not just go away when one stops competing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: More is also known today about latent injuries that emerge long after one's sporting days are over.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is an increasing concern, especially in contact and collision sports, about chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a type of dementia caused by repeated head injuries that affect the brain's function over time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This knowledge has led to concerns amongst sporting bodies across the world and some have implemented changes to the rules of training and sports to reduce the risk to athletes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, how well covered are our national athletes against such long-term or latent injuries?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is a joke about the Football Association of Singapore in this context – that FAS stands for "Forget After Service".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To be fair to the FAS, we have noted their recent efforts to provide career support to former players, which is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even so, the injuries and their long-term impact on function and quality of life remain.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A friend of mine who used to be a national hockey player, reflected on his life and the injuries he sustained and concluded that it was simply not worth it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While they commit to sporting excellence, their careers and other life decisions may be put on hold.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Their education may get delayed and they may lose work or business opportunities in the prime of their lives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It will also not be possible to trace back the amount of personal and family resources ploughed into training and getting to the levels they have achieved.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is one low-hanging fruit that I think we can and must do.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a gesture is appropriate as it acknowledges the physical toil that highly competitive sports take on one's well-being and that it is only right that society contributes more to those who have served to bring glory to the nation on the world stage.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since our national athletes are covered while serving, these subsidies should kick in after they have retired from representing Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As to who should qualify for such coverage, this should be further discussed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One possibility is to include Singaporeans who have represented the nation in any internationally recognised sport for at least a year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As to how to peg the amount of subsidies, this should be worked out.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What is important is that the subsidies lessen the out-of-pocket healthcare expenses of former national athletes, compared to other citizens.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even a further subsidy of just 10% or 20% more would be a powerful signal that society has not forgotten about them and respects their sacrifice and service.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To manage the cost to the national budget, the scheme should be scoped in terms of who should qualify and what the quantum of subsidies should be.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for the composition of the task force, I would suggest the inclusion of medical and sports science scholars and professionals who would advise on the types of injuries and conditions that are associated with competitive sports.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It should also include Government officials from the relevant agencies, such as SportSG and the Ministries of Health and Finance.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I can assure the House and the public that I have no pecuniary interest in this matter as he pays his own medical bills.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In my speech, I have focused on how we should do right for our national athletes in terms of supporting their healthcare needs over their lifetimes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wish to conclude by quoting the American running legend, Carl Lewis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He once said, "I want to be remembered as a person who felt that there was no limitation to what the human body and mind can do and be the inspiration to lead people to do things they never hoped to do." Sports do that – uplifting all of us in good times and bad.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For the pride and joy that our national athletes have brought us, we can do this bit more for them.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And by "sports" in this context, I mean sports in which our fellow countrymen and women don the national colours, wear the national flag on their sleeves or chests and go out there and compete.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Sports, in this way, are a mirror that reflects the heart and soul of our nation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I wish to make two points around this theme.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, sports reflect our values as a people – whether we only celebrate success, achievements, outcomes or whether we value equally or perhaps, even more, the process, journey and pursuit of excellence.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It reflects whether we are fair-weather fans who only partake in our fellow countrymen and women's victories or whether we stand by them all the way, through their ups and downs, and let them know that we are there for them as they give their all for us and for the nation, day in, day out, in training and in competition.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: What should success – what should a broader conversation on our goals in sports, as a nation, beyond medals and victories – look like?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this regard, I support what my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Darryl David, said earlier about helping our athletes to cope with stress.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: While we have high hopes for our athletes, we must be careful that these do not add to the stress and demands on our athletes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I am glad to note that the Singapore Sports Institute (SSI) and the National Youth Sports Institute (NYSI) have been organising and committing their resources to do just these.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But, ultimately, while we have expectations of our athletes' performance, achievements and success, let us also celebrate their journey, their pursuit of excellence, their pushing of boundaries and their maximum potential to become – again, in Mr Darryl David's words – the best version of themselves and let us support them in their downs as much as their ups.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think that is how we, as a nation, should show up for our athletes and that should underpin our goals for sports in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Second, if sports are to be a mirror that reflects the heart and soul of our society, it must mean that sports are a national project that involves all of us – athletes, sports entities, individuals, corporate supporters, civic society, alongside the Government – all of us coming together, for each and every sport, but in different ways for different sports, according to their different contexts and needs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And this national project will be a constant work in progress, constantly evolving, but all of us, coming together, that is the key and in different ways, for different sports.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Specifically, for emerging sports and niche sports, all of us got to find a way to come together and support these sports because resources of the whole ecosystem are finite and we cannot avoid the need to prioritise.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: All of us got to come together and find sensible, creative ways to best support emerging and niche sports.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I am glad to see that the Government is doing its part and playing a very active role in supporting emerging and niche sports.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, let me talk a little bit about this.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Take skydiving or, more precisely, competitive indoor skydiving.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is quite niche, certainly not for everyone.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I applaud SportSG for taking this broader view to the spexScholarship to more closely support our young Singaporeans' diverse ambitions and aspirations across various niches.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Or take sport climbing, break dancing, or breaking for short, and skateboarding.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But I know that the NYSI has started engaging our young talents in these sports even before they become part of the Major Games programmes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For example, as early as 2017, the NYSI has already started supporting skateboarder Shadiq, who was at that time only 16 years old, by sending him to the UK Talent Inspiration Programme.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Today, the Institute has a speed climbing wall which our climbers use regularly to hone their skills.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And corporates and Singaporeans at large can also play a part by contributing to the Athletes' Inspire Fund (AIF), to support these athletes to represent Singapore at international competitions.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For emerging sports, tchoukball is a good example.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And before I carry on, I thought it is important that I raise this factual clarification after listening both the speeches of hon Members Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Leon Perera.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, they have NSA status and they are recognised as an NSA.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I thought this is important and a basic clarification that I thought I should make.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The President of TBAS, Mr Delane Lim, happens to be my resident.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, through my conversations with him, I have learnt a lot about the fascinating journey of tchoukball in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And what struck me about their journey were two things: one, the passion of Delane, his team at the Association, his athletes and the entire tchoukball community for the sport; two, the strength of the support of corporates and individuals that the Association has been able to galvanise throughout their journey so far.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Their latest fundraising campaign I heard was very successful.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I am heartened to see this and I think this story of how everyone has been coming together to support and play a part in the achievements of the national tchoukball teams is something that we should be equally proud of, quite apart from the team's achievements themselves.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I understand that the Government has been playing a very active role, too, alongside the athletes, the NSA and civil society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Association is not only driving our national excellence in tchoukball.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is also looking to put Singapore on the regional and world maps for tchoukball.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, they are also looking to host regional and world tournaments and I understand SportSG has provided key support for these aspirations.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I will be going down to support the national teams and the Association in these tournaments and I look forward to a wonderful showing of skills and heart from the teams.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I believe sports are a mirror that reflects the heart and soul of our nation and our society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This means that success and our broader goals as a nation with regard to sports must be about how we support every sport and every sportsperson, every athlete, at every step of the journey, whether the sport or sportsperson is emerging, reaching a peak, staying at the peak or, indeed, going through the important and necessary valleys and downslopes en route to the peaks.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is about how we show up throughout the journey.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is also, fundamentally, about coming together – athletes, sports entities, individuals and corporate supporters, civic society, alongside the Government, forging a compact.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Inevitably, the Government will be the biggest animal in the jungle.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But precisely because of this, it behoves the Government to exercise wisdom while playing an active role in the ecosystem, always looking to get things done through partnerships, indeed, enabling, empowering and strengthening various partners and stakeholders in the ecosystem and finding different ways to go far together in different sports, including in emerging and niche sports.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I have to stress this: the basic orientation for us has to be to go far together, rather than to go fast on any of our own.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We play the long game; we take the long view.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And the final point, Madam, because sports are a mirror that reflects the heart and soul of our nation and our society, fundamentally, sports should unite, not divide.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Therefore, we do not need to exaggerate differences when there are few and we should celebrate common ground where there is plenty of such.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this debate, I have seen and heard, first and foremost, a shared sense and a shared desire for sports in Singapore to help our athletes reach their maximal potential, to rally our communities and to strengthen our sense of togetherness and national pride.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, for these reasons, I support the spirit of the original Motion but I also support the amendments to the Motion as proposed by Mr Darryl David, to better reflect and encapsulate what, ultimately, we all want for sports in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It is a powerful force that can shape a nation's identity, unite its people and even transform the world.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Sporting achievements matter to a nation because they go beyond more athletic prowess.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They embody the values, aspirations and spirit of the people, whether it is the roar of the stadium packed with loyal fans or the sight of the national team standing proudly on the podium.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Sporting events have the power to bring a nation to life in ways that few other things can.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Through sports, nations learn about teamwork, perseverance and the importance of hard work.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Sporting achievements inspire young people to pursue their dreams and they serve as a reminder to all that, with dedication and commitment, anything is possible.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In short, sporting achievements matter to a nation because they are a source of pride, a symbol of hope and a celebration of what we can accomplish when we come together as one.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Over the years, I have had the opportunity to function in various roles and capacities in the sports industry.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Sports have had a significant impact on my being and, because of this, I am thankful to join the debate on this Motion put forth by Members Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Muhamad Faisal Abdul Manap about sports.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: And this is my last speech as a Nominated Member of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This Motion is very wide and covers an array of complex topics and I would like to ask the hon Members in this House to indulge me as I plunge into my own sporting journey and share my experiences and thoughts on Singapore's sporting ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This is a very comprehensive list and I hope I did not miss anyone out.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: But SNOC and NSAs are non-government organisations that cooperate with Government and non-Government bodies to fulfil their objectives.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: SNOC promotes the general interest of sports in Singapore to develop and protect the Olympic movement in Singapore and to plan, select and administer any Singapore team with respect to the International Olympic Committee (IOC) or Olympic Games Federation, other organisations and the like.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: NSAs are concerned with the promotion of the development of the sport in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I can broadly segment this out into three groups.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The first is sports initiation; the second is development; and the third is high performance.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: And as hon Member Ms Poh Li San has alluded in her speech, grassroots and community sports are important to the pipeline of our athletes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: A more senior sports administrator told me – and I hold this to heart – that without our pipeline, we have no lifeline.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: At the sports initiation level, the aim is to introduce sports and equip participants with foundational skills in order to enjoy sports safely.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore Aquatics works with SwimSafer as well as members and other private sector partners to implement learn-to-swim programmes for the public.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore Aquatics trains the coaches, together with Coach SG and Safe Sport.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This course equips coaches with the necessary pedagogical skills to enable swimmers at a young age to attain the skills in a safe and productive environment.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: From a regulatory perspective, Singapore Aquatics has a registry of coaches which it maintains with Coach SG, and coaches who go against the Code of Conduct may be suspended.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: However, this enforcement is effective primarily on coaches that practise in public pools or MOE programmes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I have raised this concern in the House.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: And I am working with MCCY on this and believe we are closer today than we were yesterday in regulating coaches who practise in private pools and condos and this will go a long way in ensuring that all coaches are competent and have the necessary safety skills and training to teach water safety safely in any environment.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: At the development level, participants take part in organised sports programmes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They learn how to train and practise and, at the more advanced levels, the athletes learn how to compete in a structured environment.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Most of the activities are done at the community level with Singapore Aquatics members, Active SG and its academies.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: And at the pinnacle of sports, Singapore Aquatics runs high-performance programmes for its national teams in its five aquatic sports – swimming, diving, artistic swimming, open water swimming and water polo.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This relates to the hiring and appointment of national coaches and technical directors, the training environment and sending teams to appropriate level competitions, nomination of athletes to SNOC for major games and selection of national teams to the World Championships.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In terms of support, the Singapore Sport Institute (SSI) provides funding and administrative support and sports science support to win at the world-class level.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: More specifically, winning at the world stage today is hard.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In previous speeches I made in Parliament, I mentioned that the athlete entourage has grown.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The demands on the athletes have also increased and the pressures remain about social media and athletes staying longer in the sport have increased the opportunity cost, which is why I believe that more needs to be done for the mental well-being of our athletes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Yes, Singapore can do it and we have proven that we can achieve, with world champions in badminton, silat, bowling and swimming.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As Members know, I was a coach of our World and Paralympic Champion Yip Pin Xiu.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Together, we achieved four world championship titles, two para golds and seven world records.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: A large part of our success was because she is, of course, a phenomenal athlete and has a great ethic.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: But, more importantly, I was able to relate – as a former athlete – and communicate to her in high-performance terms.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I was also able to manage myself under high-pressure situations.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Oftentimes, we talked about the athlete entourage but the coaches' entourage is also just as important.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As we develop more high-performance coaches, we should also look at their mental well-being as well.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Coaches are with the athletes every hour, every step of the way, every stroke.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Travelling with the athletes overseas at competitions and camps, for every moment the coach is not on deck or on the track, they are thinking about the next session and how to extract the best out of their athletes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This is why I would like to ask SSI to consider supporting our coaches and administrators as well.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: At this juncture, I would also like to address the hon Member Mr Leong Mun Wai's comments on Soh Rui Yong's non-selection for the 2023 Asian Games.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I had earlier clarified with the hon Leader of the Opposition that Mr Soh can continue to represent Singapore at the Singapore Athletics' meets.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: On the non-selection of the Asian Games, SNOC had given Mr Soh a second chance to compete at the SEA Games in Cambodia after the Appeals Committee considered Singapore Athletics' nomination of Mr Soh.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The Appeals Committee was satisfied and sent Mr Soh to the 2023 SEA Games.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Soh signed the Letter of Undertaking; and in spite of that, he made disparaging comments on social media after the SEA Games.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: On the topic of disability sports, I believe things are moving forward with the Disability Master Plan.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We see more para-athletes doing well at the international level.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that with the ActiveSG Academies, access to disability's specific sports programmes is being implemented.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I am also happy to note that private sports clubs like ART Aquatics and Pin Xiu's Apex Swim Club are providing swimming programmes for children with special needs.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: High-performance sports take up the most resources at NSAs and NSAs work closely with SSI to plan and implement policies for its athletes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As some hon Members, such as Ms Poh Li San and Mdm Deputy Speaker Jessica Tan, who are Presidents of NSAs would know, SportSG looks at annual grant funding in periods of three to five years.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Although the funding is assessed and disbursed annually, NSAs need to take a long-term view on athlete development.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Key sports are also included in the 2024, 2028 meetings where NSAs work together with Sport SG to look at accomplishments at the world and Olympic levels.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, Singapore Aquatics is already identifying athletes and preparing these athletes for 2029.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Because of this planning required by SportSG, NSAs, like Singapore Aquatics, can see to their continued success.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I would like to join Members Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Muhamad Faisal Abdul Manap in their Motion to celebrate the achievements of our athletes at the 32nd Southeast Asian Games and the 12th ASEAN Para Games in Cambodia.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In 2000, at the age of 18, I represented Singapore at the Sydney Olympic Games.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: That year, I was ranked first in Asia in the 200-metre freestyle.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I have been the CEO of an NSA and currently the President of one.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I have had the good fortune of being a world champion coach.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I was on SNOC's exco and I am serving in various capacities in international sporting organisations.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I have seen and experienced various systems and models internationally.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: There is no perfect system in the world, but this is a system that works in Singapore for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I am excited by the amendments to the Motion that we will continue to not only refine it for our needs and the changing requirements but also to have a commitment from this House that we will commit to realising our ambitions for high-performance sports over the coming decade.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I am thrilled to support these amendments to the Motion.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I have the following suggestions – so, please bear with me.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Many NSAs and clubs require facilities around programmes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I would be the first to say that I have never swum faster than I did after National Service (NS), not because I was not allowed the time to train but because I sustained a career-ending injury right before enlistment.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I think this goes a long way to show appreciation for our athletes who have sacrificed so much.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that NS is essential and every male Singaporean has to do it.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I believe these schemes are fair and our athletes have been very receptive to the flexibility given to them to train, prepare and compete.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I spoke at the Committee of Supply (COS) about how Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) should play a part in teaching students how to work and exercise.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, I would like to acknowledge the hon Member Gerald Giam's comments about parents and how important a part they play in a child's sporting journey.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As a parent of a young child myself, I hope to be a sporting parent like Mr Giam.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot overstate the importance of parents in Singapore's sporting success.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: At the highest level of competition, sports inspire us with the incredible feats of athleticism and determination that are possible when we push ourselves to our limits.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond the spectacle of competition, sports promote discipline, dedication and perseverance.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Athletes who train and compete at that level, learn to set goals, work hard and overcome adversity.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They develop their skills and abilities to reach new heights of achievements, showing us what is possible when we apply ourselves to a challenge.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, sports provide powerful role models for our young people, inspiring them to pursue their passions and believe in themselves.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They show us that with hard work, dedication and perseverance, we can achieve great things and make a positive impact on the world around us.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They provide a common ground where people can connect and share in the joy of competition and achievement, fostering friendship and goodwill amongst individuals and nations alike.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Through sports, Singaporeans can push ourselves to new levels of achievement and inspire others to do the same, building a brighter future for us and generations to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just a quick series of questions for the NMP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: He raised the matter of Rui Yong again and I think my speech made it quite clear where I stood on the matter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just to confirm the point, I think he put the question as to whether Rui Yong has been disparaging and so forth.

text: I have not made the point in my speech that discipline and all these other important things in sports are not important.

text: But I would like to ask the Member does he advocate a system where it is "two strikes and you are out"?

text: I mean, the episode can be resolved in other ways and I have made my point why I think it could be resolved in other ways.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Would he join me in advocating for more dispute resolution mechanisms that can build bridges and, in his words, "unite" rather than "divide"?
